title: Incident Response Lifecycle (NIST 800-61)
summary: The four-phase incident response lifecycle from NIST Special Publication 800-61 — preparation, detection and analysis, containment/eradication/recovery, and post-incident activity — taught as an operator's playbook for an endpoint fleet. You will learn IR roles, how to build a playbook before anything burns, and how to run a tabletop exercise on a fictional 2 AM ransomware scenario.
objectives: Describe the four NIST 800-61 incident response phases and what belongs in each.
Distinguish incident precursors from indicators and triage alerts by impact and recoverability.
Choose containment actions that stop damage without destroying evidence.
Sequence eradication and recovery so the root cause is gone before systems return.
Run a blameless post-incident review and write an after-action report with owned action items.
Design and facilitate a tabletop exercise for a ransomware scenario.

notes.title: The four phases: NIST SP 800-61's incident response lifecycle
notes.body: NIST Special Publication 800-61 organizes incident response into four phases that loop, not a straight line: (1) Preparation — everything built before an incident, from team roles to tested backups; (2) Detection and Analysis — noticing something wrong, confirming it is real, and scoping how bad it is; (3) Containment, Eradication, and Recovery — stopping the damage, removing the cause, and bringing systems back safely; (4) Post-Incident Activity — learning from what happened so it does not repeat. The phases feed back into each other: analysis during containment often sends you back to re-scope, and post-incident findings rewrite your preparation. Worked example: at 2:00 AM a monitoring alert fires — ransomware encrypting files on three workstations. Detection and analysis (2:00-2:40): you confirm the alert is real, find the initial phishing email, and discover 11 more hosts with the same malware beaconing. Containment (2:40-4:00): you isolate all 14 hosts from the network but leave them powered on to preserve memory. Eradication (day 2): you identify the malicious scheduled task and rogue account, remove them fleet-wide, and patch the exploited vulnerability. Recovery (days 3-5): you restore the file server from a tested backup and bring departments back in priority order with extra monitoring. Post-incident (week 2): the review finds the phishing email bypassed the filter — action item: tune the filter and run a targeted phishing drill. Common mistakes: treating the phases as a checklist you visit once (real incidents bounce between detection and containment for hours); skipping preparation and improvising under pressure; and jumping to eradication — wiping machines — before scoping, which destroys evidence and leaves the entry point open for reinfection. A detail worth internalizing: the phases are drawn as a cycle because real incidents refuse to stay in one box. You contain three hosts, then firewall logs reveal a fourth beaconing host you missed — you are back in detection and analysis, re-scoping, before containment resumes. The current revision of the guidance is NIST SP 800-61 Revision 2, and its core message has not changed across revisions: coordination and preparation matter more than tools. Another worked micro-example: during eradication of the ransomware case, the team discovers the phishing email also reached the billing department's shared mailbox, which auto-forwards to an external accountant. That single finding re-opens scoping (is the accountant's machine compromised?), extends containment (block the forwarding rule), and adds a post-incident action item (review all mailbox forwarding rules quarterly). One artifact, three phases touched. Operator gotcha for the exam-minded: when a question asks 'which phase,' look for the verb — building, testing, and documenting are preparation; confirming and scoping are detection and analysis; isolating and blocking are containment; removing root cause is eradication; restoring service is recovery; reviewing and reporting are post-incident. The verbs decide.

notes.title: Preparation: everything that must exist before the alert
notes.body: Preparation is the phase you control completely, and it decides how the other three go. A prepared organization has: named IR roles with backups (who is incident commander at 2 AM, and who is their backup); an incident response playbook with call trees and decision authority (who can authorize taking the file server offline); out-of-band communication — a way to talk that does not depend on the systems under attack (a separate chat channel, phone tree, or even a conference bridge number printed on paper); tooling ready to go (EDR console access, forensic imaging tools, known-good OS install media, clean backup verification); and relationships established in advance (legal counsel, HR for insider cases, law enforcement contacts, your cyber-insurance carrier's breach hotline). Worked example: a one-page prep checklist for a 150-endpoint clinic. Roles: incident commander (IT manager), technical lead (you), communications lead (office manager), scribe (whoever is free — they log every decision with timestamps). Contacts: MSP after-hours number, backup vendor support, cyber-insurance breach line, local FBI field office. Tooling: EDR admin credentials in a sealed envelope, two USB drives with clean Windows install media, a 2 TB external drive for forensic images, the phone-tree printed and taped inside the server room. Cadence: tabletop exercise quarterly, backup restore test monthly, contact list verified every six months. Operator gotchas: the playbook that lives only in someone's head is not a playbook; credentials for your IR tools must not be stored solely in the password manager that lives on the compromised network — keep an offline copy; and never assume the backup works — an untested backup is a rumor, so restore-test on schedule and record the result. Two preparation artifacts separate mature teams from improvisers: the jump bag and the tested restore. The jump bag — physical or virtual — holds everything the technical lead needs in the first hour: a laptop with forensic tools, write-blocker, external drives, clean OS media, console cables, and the printed phone tree. Build yours before you need it; during the incident is the wrong time to discover your USB drive is corrupted. On backups, preparation means proving the restore, not assuming it: schedule monthly restore tests of a sample system and a sample file share, record the result (success, duration, data integrity check), and store the log where the incident team can find it at 2 AM. A backup that has never been restored is a hope, not a control. Also prepare your evidence handling in advance: designate where forensic images go (an encrypted external drive in the safe, with a custody log taped to it), decide your hashing standard (SHA-256), and confirm you have legal's guidance on what to preserve if the incident might involve employee misconduct. Final gotcha: preparation decays. People change roles, phone numbers change, tools get replaced. Put a six-month expiry on the contact list and the playbook review, with a named owner — otherwise your beautiful plan is three years out of date when the alert fires.

notes.title: Detection and analysis: is this actually an incident?
notes.body: NIST 800-61 distinguishes precursors — signs an incident may occur in the future (a vulnerability scan against your firewall, a threat intel report about ransomware targeting healthcare) — from indicators — signs an incident is occurring or has occurred (an EDR alert for credential dumping, a user report of encrypted files, outbound traffic to a known command-and-control server). Detection sources include your own alerts, users calling the help desk, and third parties (an ISP or a partner telling you they see malicious traffic from your network). Analysis then answers three questions: is it real (triage out false positives), what is the scope (one host or fifty), and what is the priority. NIST suggests prioritizing by functional impact (how much of the business is down), information impact (was sensitive data accessed or stolen), and recoverability (can we rebuild from clean backups, or is this existential). Worked example: 9:00 AM, your ThreatLocker Detect-style console shows one alert — 'powershell.exe launched by winword.exe' on a single workstation, blocked. Triage: real behavior, but blocked before damage; scope is one host; priority moderate — you investigate the email that delivered the document. Contrast: 2:00 AM, fourteen hosts beaconing to an external IP and file shares encrypting. Scope is fleet-wide, functional impact is severe, information impact unknown — that is a full incident, wake everyone up. Common mistakes: treating every alert as a five-alarm fire (alert fatigue burns out your team and teaches everyone to ignore the console); the opposite — assuming a single blocked alert needs no follow-up (the block stopped this attempt, but the phishing email that delivered it may have reached fifty inboxes); and scoping by gut feel instead of evidence — always check: same email to other users, same hash on other hosts, same outbound connections in firewall logs. Dwell time — the gap between initial compromise and detection — is the statistic that should haunt you. Industry reports have historically measured dwell in weeks or months for incidents discovered by third parties; your goal is to drive yours toward hours through better detection and user reporting. Practically, scoping is where analysis lives or dies. Beyond checking which users opened the attachment, pull firewall and DNS logs for the indicators: which internal hosts resolved the malicious domain, which hosts made the outbound connection, and when did each start. One clinic case: the EDR showed three encrypted hosts, but DNS logs showed eleven hosts resolving the attacker's domain over the prior week — the true scope was eleven, and the extra eight were caught before encryption because someone looked at DNS. Another analysis discipline: separate the signal from the noise in the first 30 minutes by assigning one person to timeline duty while others contain — the timeline builder records every confirmed fact with a timestamp, which prevents the team from acting on rumors. Common tuning mistake: after a noisy false positive, teams silence the rule instead of tuning it. Silencing deletes future true positives; tuning (adding the legitimate admin tool's path as an exception, narrowing the condition) keeps the detection alive. Every alert disposition — true positive, benign true positive, false positive — should feed back into detection engineering, which is preparation for the next incident.

notes.title: Containment: stop the bleeding without destroying evidence
notes.body: Containment means preventing the incident from spreading while preserving evidence for analysis. NIST describes short-term containment (isolate the host from the network right now) versus long-term containment (temporary firewall rules, disabling VPN accounts, blocking malicious domains at DNS — measures that hold for days while you work). The golden rule: contain first, but contain in a way that keeps your options open. Pulling the network cable or using EDR network-isolation keeps the machine running, which preserves memory evidence; powering the machine off destroys RAM contents and can trigger anti-forensic behavior. Decision criteria for how aggressive to be: how fast is it spreading (ransomware encrypting shares = isolate immediately, even if it disrupts users), whether you understand the mechanism yet (if not, isolate broadly), and business impact of the containment itself (taking the file server offline at month-end close needs executive sign-off — which is why preparation defined who can authorize it). Worked example: ransomware confirmed on three workstations at 2 AM. Step 1: network-isolate all three via EDR (or unplug Ethernet / disable Wi-Fi if no EDR) — do NOT shut them down. Step 2: check the file server for encryption activity and snapshot it. Step 3: block the command-and-control domains at the firewall so any undiscovered infected host cannot receive instructions. Step 4: disable the compromised user accounts in Active Directory. Only after scoping is complete do you move to eradication. Operator gotchas: wiping a machine 'to stop it' before imaging destroys your only copy of the malware and the timeline; telling the whole company 'we have ransomware' before containment is complete can tip off an insider threat actor; and documenting every containment action with timestamps matters — the post-incident review and any legal follow-up will need that log. Containment decisions vary by host role, and the playbook should say so in advance. A user workstation: isolate aggressively, minimal business impact. A file server: isolate, but coordinate — taking it offline halts the whole clinic, so the incident commander weighs encryption spread against business halt, and the answer is usually 'isolate now, the encryption will halt the business worse.' A domain controller: do not isolate blindly — authentication for the entire network depends on it; instead block the malicious outbound traffic at the firewall, disable compromised accounts, and monitor closely while planning a controlled rebuild. These are decisions you want pre-made, not invented at 3 AM. Communication during containment follows the same discipline: the communications lead sends timed updates ('containment in progress, next update at 04:00') to a defined distribution list, and nobody else freelances status reports. A second containment gotcha: watch for the attacker's counter-move. Ransomware crews monitor for containment — when hosts go dark, they may accelerate encryption on remaining hosts or trigger pre-planted persistence. That is why containment should be as simultaneous as possible across the scoped host set rather than trickled one machine at a time. Document the containment timestamp per host; the post-incident review will compare 'scope at containment' versus 'final scope' to judge whether containment was fast and complete enough.

notes.title: Eradication and recovery: remove the cause, restore safely
notes.body: Eradication removes the root cause; recovery brings systems back into production. The order is non-negotiable: never recover before eradication is verified, or you will reinfect clean systems. Eradication means identifying every persistence mechanism and removing all of them — the malicious scheduled task AND the rogue local account AND the backdoored service, not just the one you found first. It also means closing the entry point: patch the exploited vulnerability, reset credentials that may have been stolen (assume all credentials on compromised hosts are burned), and remove the phishing email from every inbox it reached. Recovery then proceeds in priority order: the most critical business functions first, each system rebuilt from known-good media or restored from a backup that predates the compromise — and that you have verified is clean. After recovery comes a period of enhanced monitoring: watch the recovered systems closely for days or weeks, because sophisticated attackers leave second-stage persistence. Worked example: after the 2 AM ransomware, eradication finds the initial access was a phishing email with a malicious attachment, and lateral movement used a stolen domain admin credential. Eradication checklist: delete the malware from all 14 hosts (or reimage them — reimaging from known-good media is the safest eradication for workstations), remove the rogue scheduled task fleet-wide via GPO audit, force-reset ALL domain passwords (the admin credential was stolen, so every credential is suspect), patch the exploited print-spooler-style vulnerability, purge the phishing email from all mailboxes. Recovery order: domain controllers first (rebuilt, not restored, if their integrity is doubted), then the file server from the last pre-incident tested backup, then departments by business priority — billing before the break room PC. Enhanced monitoring: EDR set to high sensitivity on recovered hosts for 30 days, plus a daily review of authentication logs. Common mistakes: recovering from a backup without confirming the backup predates the compromise (attackers dwell for weeks — restore from a backup taken during dwell and you restore the attacker); resetting only the obviously compromised accounts; and declaring victory the day systems come back instead of after the monitoring period. Credential resets deserve their own eradication sub-plan, done in tiers. Tier 1 — known-compromised accounts (the phished user, any account seen in lateral movement): reset immediately during containment. Tier 2 — privileged accounts (domain admins, service accounts): reset during eradication even without direct evidence of compromise, because credential theft is quiet and the cost of missing one is another incident. Tier 3 — all remaining user passwords: forced reset during recovery, communicated clearly so the help desk is not drowned. Service accounts need special care: resetting them without updating every dependent service causes outages, so inventory service accounts during preparation, not during the incident. Validating backups before recovery is equally tiered: confirm the backup timestamp predates the earliest known malicious activity (not just the encryption date — dwell matters), verify integrity with a test restore of a non-critical system first, and scan restored data with current detections before returning it to production. Enhanced monitoring after recovery should be specific, not vibes: EDR in heightened sensitivity on recovered hosts for 30 days, daily review of authentication logs for the first two weeks, firewall alerts on any outbound connection to the previously seen malicious infrastructure, and a weekly scope re-check for the first month. Eradication is only verified when the monitoring period ends clean — declare victory then, not on recovery day.

notes.title: Post-incident activity: the blameless review and the after-action report
notes.body: Post-incident activity is where the incident pays for itself in lessons. NIST 800-61 calls for a lessons-learned meeting held soon after the incident — while memories are fresh — with one ground rule: it is blameless. The moment the review becomes about who clicked the phishing link, people stop telling the truth and you learn nothing. The meeting reconstructs a full timeline (when did the phishing email arrive, when did execution start, when was it detected, when was containment complete), then asks: what went well, what went poorly, what surprised us, and what will we change. Every lesson becomes an action item with a named owner and a due date, or it evaporates. The after-action report (AAR) documents all of this: executive summary, timeline, impact assessment, response actions taken, what worked, gaps found, and the action-item list. Also collect metrics: mean time to detect (MTTD — first malicious action to detection), mean time to respond/contain (MTTR — detection to containment), and scope at containment versus final scope (did it keep spreading after you acted?). Worked example: AAR skeleton for the ransomware incident. Executive summary: 'On Oct 3, ransomware encrypted 14 workstations and one file share; contained within 2 hours of detection; no evidence of data exfiltration; full recovery in 5 days.' Timeline: 01:12 phishing email delivered; 06:40 user opened attachment; 06:41 execution and lateral movement began; 02:00 next-day... (reconstructed from logs). What worked: EDR network-isolation contained hosts in minutes; the phone tree reached the full team by 2:30 AM. Gaps: phishing filter missed the email (action: tune filter, owner: email admin, due: Oct 20); no network segmentation between workstations and file server (action: VLAN plan, owner: you, due: Nov 30); backups had never been restore-tested (action: monthly restore tests, owner: backup admin, due: ongoing). Metrics: MTTD 19 hours (dwell before encryption was noticed), MTTR 2 hours. Operator gotcha: the review must include the people who were in the trenches, not just managers — the help-desk tech who took the first user call often has the most important observation. The after-action report has two audiences and should be written for both: a one-page executive summary (what happened, business impact, what we are changing) and the technical appendix (full timeline, artifacts, indicators). Distribute the technical findings beyond the IR team — detection engineering needs the indicators, IT operations needs the hardening tasks, and training needs the user-facing lesson. Track every action item to closure in whatever system the organization actually checks; an action item that lives only in the AAR document is decorative. Review the metrics quarterly across incidents: is MTTD trending down? Are repeat root causes appearing (the third phishing incident this year means the email control, not the users, is the problem)? Feed systemic findings into the risk register so leadership sees incident lessons as risk reduction, not just IT homework. A final post-incident discipline: the 'pre-mortem' for the next incident. Ask the team, 'It is six months from now and we are breached again through the same vector — what did we fail to do after this incident?' The answers become your highest-priority action items, because they represent the lessons you are most likely to let slide. Incident response maturity is not measured by how well you handle the incident — it is measured by how few of your action items are still open at the next tabletop.

notes.title: IR roles and designing the 2 AM ransomware tabletop
notes.body: A tabletop exercise is a discussion-based walkthrough of a scenario — no systems are touched, but the team talks through exactly what they would do, which exposes gaps in the playbook before a real incident does. Core IR roles to assign: the incident commander (owns decisions and the clock — not the keyboard; their job is prioritization and authorization), the technical lead (owns the hands-on investigation and containment actions), the communications lead (owns internal updates, executive briefings, and any external notifications — one voice, no freelancing), and the scribe (logs every decision, action, and timestamp — this log becomes the backbone of the after-action report). Optional: legal advisor, HR representative (for insider scenarios), and an executive sponsor who can authorize disruptive containment. Designing the exercise: write a scenario narrative (the 2 AM ransomware), define objectives ('test our containment decision process and our out-of-band comms'), then script injects — new facts delivered at intervals that force decisions. Ground rules: this is a safe space, there are no wrong answers, and 'we would call the MSP' is a valid answer only if someone actually has the number. Worked example: three injects for the ransomware tabletop. Inject 1 (T+0): 'It is 2:00 AM. Your phone rings — the monitoring system reports ransomware encrypting files on three workstations. What do you do in the first 15 minutes?' (Tests: call tree, initial containment, who declares an incident.) Inject 2 (T+30 min): 'The file server is now showing encrypted files, and the EDR console is unreachable — the admin credentials you have do not work.' (Tests: out-of-band comms, credential compromise assumptions, escalation authority.) Inject 3 (T+2 hours): 'A local news station calls asking about a rumored cyberattack at the clinic.' (Tests: communications lead discipline, executive notification, no ad-lib statements.) The facilitator keeps time, the scribe captures everything, and the debrief at the end converts observations into playbook updates. Operator gotcha: the most valuable tabletop finding is almost always embarrassingly basic — 'nobody had the MSP's after-hours number' — which is exactly why you run it before the real thing. Facilitation tips that separate a useful tabletop from a pleasant chat: keep the scenario plausible but uncomfortable — the exercise should find the gap, not confirm the plan. Time-box each inject (15-20 minutes of discussion) and cut off rambling with 'noted — what is the decision?' Inject information asymmetrically the way real incidents do: the technical lead learns the EDR is down before the incident commander does, forcing a communication test. Include at least one inject that invalidates the plan ('the phone tree's first three numbers go to voicemail') because plans always fail at the seams. For remote teams, run the tabletop over the actual out-of-band channel you would use in an incident — testing the bridge line is part of the exercise. Evaluation is observation, not grading: the facilitator and scribe watch for decision latency (how long before someone declares an incident?), authority clarity (did anyone actually make the call, or did the group drift?), communication discipline (did updates flow through the comms lead?), and evidence thinking (did anyone say 'preserve memory before wiping'?). Convert every observation into a playbook edit within a week, and re-run the same scenario in six months to verify the fixes stuck. One exercise per quarter, rotating scenarios (ransomware, business email compromise, insider data theft, third-party breach notification), builds the muscle memory that makes the real 2 AM call feel familiar instead of chaotic.

cards.front: Name the four NIST 800-61 incident response phases in order.
cards.back: 1. Preparation. 2. Detection and Analysis. 3. Containment, Eradication, and Recovery. 4. Post-Incident Activity.

cards.front: Precursor vs. indicator — what is the difference?
cards.back: A precursor signals an incident MIGHT happen (e.g., a scan against your firewall). An indicator signals one IS happening or HAS happened (e.g., an EDR alert for credential dumping).

cards.front: What three factors does NIST 800-61 suggest for prioritizing an incident?
cards.back: Functional impact (business disruption), information impact (data accessed/stolen), and recoverability (can we rebuild from clean backups).

cards.front: Short-term vs. long-term containment — give an example of each.
cards.back: Short-term: network-isolate the infected host right now. Long-term: firewall rules blocking C2 domains and disabling compromised VPN accounts for days while you work.

cards.front: Why isolate a ransomware host instead of powering it off?
cards.back: Isolation stops spread while keeping the machine running, preserving memory (RAM) evidence. Powering off destroys RAM contents and timeline evidence.

cards.front: Eradication vs. recovery — which comes first and why?
cards.back: Eradication first: remove every persistence mechanism and close the entry point. Recovering first risks reinfecting clean systems from the still-present attacker.

cards.front: What is 'out-of-band communication' and why does IR need it?
cards.back: A communication channel independent of the compromised systems (separate chat, phone tree, printed bridge number) — because the attacker may control or monitor your normal email/chat.

cards.front: What is the incident commander's job during an incident?
cards.back: Own decisions and the clock: prioritization, authorizing disruptive containment, and coordination — not doing the technical keyboard work.

cards.front: What is a tabletop exercise?
cards.back: A discussion-based walkthrough of a scenario where the team talks through their response without touching systems — it exposes playbook gaps before a real incident.

cards.front: What goes into an after-action report (AAR)?
cards.back: Executive summary, full timeline, impact assessment, response actions, what worked, gaps found, and action items each with a named owner and due date.

cards.front: Define MTTD and MTTR in incident response.
cards.back: MTTD = mean time to detect (first malicious action to detection). MTTR = mean time to respond/contain (detection to containment).

cards.front: What is the ground rule of the lessons-learned meeting?
cards.back: It is blameless — no fault-finding about who clicked or who missed it, so people tell the truth and the team actually learns.

quiz.q: According to NIST 800-61, which phase includes building the IR playbook, defining roles, and testing backups?
choices: Preparation
Detection and Analysis
Containment, Eradication, and Recovery
Post-Incident Activity
quiz.explain: Preparation is everything built before an incident: roles, playbooks, call trees, tooling, tested backups, and relationships with legal, HR, and law enforcement.

quiz.q: A threat intel report warns that ransomware crews are targeting healthcare clinics this month. In NIST terms this is a:
choices: Precursor
Indicator
Confirmed incident
False positive
quiz.explain: A precursor signals an incident may occur in the future. An indicator would be evidence it is occurring now, such as an EDR alert or encrypted files.

quiz.q: Ransomware is actively encrypting a file share at 2 AM. Your FIRST containment action should be:
choices: Network-isolate the affected hosts while leaving them powered on
Power off all affected machines immediately
Wipe and reimage the affected workstations
Email all staff warning them about the ransomware
quiz.explain: Isolation stops the spread while preserving memory evidence. Powering off destroys RAM; wiping destroys all evidence and skips scoping; mass email before containment risks tipping off an insider and causes panic.

quiz.q: During scoping you find the phishing email reached 50 inboxes but only 3 users opened the attachment. What does good analysis require next?
choices: Check the other 47 mailboxes and hosts for signs of execution before declaring scope
Assume only the 3 are affected and start wiping them
Delete the email from all mailboxes and close the incident
Wait to see if more alerts fire
quiz.explain: Scope must be evidence-driven: verify each recipient's host for execution artifacts. Assuming scope from the alert count alone is how reinfections happen.

quiz.q: Which eradication step is most commonly skipped, leading to reinfection?
choices: Removing ALL persistence mechanisms and closing the entry point (patching, credential resets, purging the phish)
Deleting the obvious malware file
Reimaging the first infected workstation
Blocking the C2 domain at the firewall
quiz.explain: Attackers plant multiple persistence mechanisms. Removing one file while leaving the rogue scheduled task, stolen credentials, and unpatched vulnerability intact guarantees a return visit.

quiz.q: When is the correct time to restore systems from backup?
choices: After eradication is verified and the backup is confirmed to predate the compromise
Immediately, to minimize downtime
Before containment, to preserve user data
Only after the lessons-learned meeting
quiz.explain: Recovering before eradication reinfects clean systems, and restoring a backup taken during attacker dwell restores the attacker. Verify both first.

quiz.q: The lessons-learned meeting should be:
choices: Blameless, held soon after the incident, with action items assigned owners and due dates
Focused on identifying who caused the incident
Delayed a few months until emotions cool
Limited to managers to save time
quiz.explain: Blameless and prompt so people tell the truth; action items without owners evaporate; frontline staff who lived it must be in the room.

quiz.q: Your EDR console is unreachable during an incident and your admin credentials fail. What preparation failure does this reveal?
choices: No offline/out-of-band copy of IR tool credentials and no tested alternate access path
Insufficient EDR licensing
Failure to buy cyber insurance
Missing vulnerability scanner
quiz.explain: Preparation requires IR tool access that survives compromise of the normal environment — offline credential copies and out-of-band access paths, tested in advance.

quiz.q: In a tabletop exercise, the facilitator announces: 'The file server is now encrypting and your EDR credentials do not work.' This is called:
choices: An inject — a new fact forcing a decision
An indicator of compromise
A precursor
Scope creep
quiz.explain: Injects are scripted developments delivered during the exercise to test decision-making under changing conditions — the core mechanic of a tabletop.

quiz.q: MTTD is 19 hours and MTTR is 2 hours for a ransomware incident. What does this tell you?
choices: Detection is the weak link — the attacker dwelled 19 hours before anyone noticed; response once detected was fast
Response was too slow
The incident was minor
Containment failed
quiz.explain: MTTD measures first-malicious-action to detection (19h dwell = detection gap); MTTR measures detection to containment (2h = strong response). Metrics direct improvement effort at detection.

items.prompt: Phase 1 of NIST 800-61?
items.explain: Roles, playbooks, tooling, tested backups — all built before an incident.

items.prompt: Phase 2 of NIST 800-61?
items.explain: Confirm it is real, triage, and scope how bad it is.

items.prompt: Phase 3 of NIST 800-61?
items.explain: Stop spread, remove the cause, restore safely — in that order.

items.prompt: Phase 4 of NIST 800-61?
items.explain: Blameless lessons-learned and the after-action report with owned action items.

items.prompt: Scan against your firewall reported by the ISP — precursor or indicator?
items.explain: It signals an incident may occur, not that one is occurring.

items.prompt: Outbound traffic to a known C2 server — precursor or indicator?
items.explain: It signals compromise is occurring or has occurred — act on it.

items.prompt: Who owns decisions and the clock during an incident?
items.explain: Prioritization and authorization — not the keyboard work.

items.prompt: Who logs every decision and timestamp during an incident?
items.explain: Their log becomes the backbone of the after-action report.

items.prompt: One blocked 'Word launched PowerShell' alert on a single host, no other signals. First move?
items.answer: Investigate as a moderate-priority lead: find the delivering email, check the host, see if the email reached other inboxes.
items.explain: The block stopped this attempt, but the delivery vector may have wider reach — scope before dismissing.

items.prompt: Ransomware encrypting shares, spreading host to host. Contain now or finish scoping first?
items.answer: Contain now — isolate affected hosts immediately, then continue scoping.
items.explain: Active spreading outranks complete scoping; you can scope from isolated hosts and logs.

items.prompt: You have isolated 6 hosts but have not found the initial access vector. Wipe them now?
items.answer: No — preserve evidence first (memory, disk image or key artifacts), find the entry point, then eradicate.
items.explain: Wiping before understanding the entry point destroys evidence and leaves the door open.

items.prompt: The CEO demands the file server back online during active containment. Who decides?
items.answer: The incident commander, using the pre-agreed authorization matrix from preparation — not the loudest voice.
items.explain: This is exactly why preparation defines who can authorize disruptive or risky actions.

items.prompt: Post-incident review reveals the backup had never been restore-tested. Write the action item.
items.answer: Action: monthly backup restore tests with recorded results. Owner: backup admin. Due: ongoing, first test within 14 days.
items.explain: Every lesson needs a named owner and a due date or it evaporates.

items.prompt: A news reporter calls during the incident asking about 'the cyberattack.' Who responds and how?
items.answer: Only the communications lead, with a prepared holding statement — no one else freelances.
items.explain: One voice prevents contradictory statements and legal exposure; preparation writes the holding statement in advance.

handsOnLab.title: Tabletop: 2 AM ransomware at a fictional clinic
handsOnLab.brief: You will design and run (solo, with a friend, or with an AI as facilitator) a tabletop exercise for a fictional 150-endpoint healthcare clinic hit by ransomware at 2 AM, then write the after-action report. This is the exact muscle the ThreatLocker panel will probe: calm, ordered incident thinking.
steps: Write the one-page scenario: 'Harborview Clinic, 150 endpoints, 2:00 AM Tuesday. Monitoring alerts: ransomware encrypting files on 3 workstations. You are the technical lead; the IT manager is incident commander.'
Draft the IR roster for the clinic: incident commander, technical lead (you), communications lead, scribe — with a backup for each role and an out-of-band contact method.
Write your preparation checklist: what should have existed before 2 AM (EDR access, offline credential copy, clean install media, phone tree, cyber-insurance breach line).
Script 4 injects on a timeline: T+0 initial alert; T+30 file server encrypting + EDR console unreachable; T+90 news reporter calls; T+4h CEO demands systems back for morning appointments.
Run the tabletop: for each inject, write down your decisions in order — first 15 minutes actions, containment calls, who you notify and when.
For inject 2, decide explicitly: isolate vs. power off, and write your evidence-preservation reasoning.
For inject 3, draft the holding statement the communications lead gives the reporter (2-3 sentences, no technical detail, no blame).
For inject 4, write how the incident commander balances patient-care pressure against reinfection risk — what returns first and under what monitoring.
Build the incident timeline from your run: detection, each decision, containment complete, eradication, recovery milestones.
Write the after-action report: executive summary, timeline, what worked, 3-5 gaps found during the exercise.
Convert each gap into an action item with a named owner and due date.
Add metrics: your MTTD (assume dwell from your scenario), your MTTR (detection to containment in the exercise), and scope at containment.
Re-read the AAR as the panel interviewer: does it show calm prioritization, evidence discipline, and blameless learning? Revise weak sections.
handsOnLab.deliverable: aar-ransomware-tabletop.md — scenario, roster, inject log with your decisions, timeline, after-action report with owned action items and metrics.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: The AAR covers all four NIST phases, names all four IR roles with backups, contains at least 3 action items each with an owner and due date, and your inject-2 decision explicitly justifies isolate-over-power-off for evidence preservation.

mockTask.q: Panel question: It is 2 AM and monitoring shows ransomware encrypting files on three workstations at a clinic. As the technical lead, what is your first move?
choices: Network-isolate the three hosts (leave them powered on), verify the alert is real, and start scoping — which other hosts got the same email or show the same behavior
Immediately wipe and reimage the three workstations to stop the encryption
Power off the entire network including servers to freeze everything in place
Send a clinic-wide email warning everyone not to open attachments
mockTask.explain: Isolate-without-power-off stops spread while preserving memory evidence; verifying and scoping before eradication prevents reinfection from an unknown entry point. Wiping destroys evidence, mass power-off kills RAM forensics, and clinic-wide email before containment causes panic and can tip off an insider.

title: Digital Forensics Fundamentals for the Endpoint
summary: What to preserve, in what order, and how — the order of volatility, disk artifacts (MFT, prefetch, event logs, registry), memory basics, timeline analysis, chain of custody, and the free toolset. Built around the question an IT infrastructure specialist actually faces: what do I save before I reimage this machine.
objectives: Apply the order of volatility to decide what to collect first on a live system.
Explain what the MFT, prefetch, event logs, and registry reveal about activity on a Windows endpoint.
Describe what lives in RAM and how to capture it without destroying it.
Build a simple timeline by correlating artifacts from multiple sources.
Maintain chain of custody with hashing, documentation, and write-blocking concepts.
Execute a pre-reimage preservation checklist on a suspect workstation.

notes.title: Order of volatility: collect the ephemeral first
notes.body: Digital evidence decays at different rates, and the order of volatility tells you what to grab first: the most fragile evidence before the most durable. From most to least volatile: CPU registers and cache (gone in microseconds — in practice you never capture these directly); RAM contents — running processes, network connections, encryption keys, injected code (gone the moment power is lost); network state — active connections, ARP cache, routing tables (changes in seconds to minutes); running process and system state (what is executing right now); then disk — files, the MFT, event logs (persist across reboots but can be overwritten); then remote logs and monitoring data; then physical configuration; then archival backups and offline media. The practical rule: on a live suspect machine, capture memory and network state before you touch the disk, and never reboot or shut down until you have decided what volatile evidence you are willing to lose. Worked example: you walk up to a workstation the EDR flagged for credential dumping. It is powered on and logged in. Correct order: (1) photograph the screen; (2) capture RAM to external media with a memory acquisition tool; (3) record active network connections and the routing/ARP tables; (4) list running processes with full command lines; (5) only then consider disk imaging or pulling event logs. Wrong order: rebooting 'to be safe' — you just destroyed the injected code, the attacker's network sessions, and possibly the encryption keys, which were the whole case. Operator gotchas: do not run your collection tools from the suspect's own disk — run them from external read-only media so you do not overwrite unallocated space; every command you run changes the system slightly, so document each one with timestamps; and if the machine is already off, do NOT power it on to 'take a look' — image the disk first, then analyze the image. Put numbers on the decay to make the ordering instinctive. RAM: total loss at power-off, partial corruption within minutes of heavy system activity as memory gets reused. Network state (ARP cache, active connections): entries age out in minutes; DHCP leases and NAT tables churn constantly. Running processes: the list is current only while the system runs — reboot and you lose which processes were active, their PIDs, and parent-child relationships. Disk: file timestamps update on access and modification, logs roll over on busy systems within days, and unallocated space gets overwritten unpredictably. Remote logs: the most durable, but only if forwarding was configured before the incident. The live-versus-dead decision matrix: system is ON and you suspect fileless activity, credential theft, or active intrusion — treat as live, capture volatile evidence first. System is OFF and was shut down cleanly — treat as dead-box: do not boot it, image the disk write-blocked. System is ON but the incident is clearly over (old malware, user already reimaged once) — targeted artifact collection from the live system is acceptable, documented. And the documentation rule that underpins all of it: every collection action gets a timestamped log entry as you perform it, not reconstructed afterward. 'I think I imaged it around 2' is not a custody record; '14:22 — began FTK Imager acquisition of \.\PhysicalDrive0 to EVIDENCE-01' is.

notes.title: Disk artifacts I: the MFT and what it remembers
notes.body: On NTFS volumes, the Master File Table (MFT) is the filesystem's index: one record per file and directory, holding the filename, timestamps, size, and where the data lives. Each MFT record carries two timestamp sets: $STANDARD_INFORMATION (SI — what Windows Explorer shows, and what timestomping malware modifies) and $FILE_NAME (FN — set at file creation and far harder to fake). That duality is a gift to investigators: if SI says a system file was 'created yesterday' but FN says 2019, someone tampered with timestamps. The MFT also remembers deleted files — deletion usually just marks the record as free without wiping it, so file names and timestamps of deleted files often survive until the record is reused. Small files may be resident (stored inside the MFT record itself); large files are non-resident (the record points to data runs elsewhere on disk). Worked example: you suspect malware dropped payload.exe into System32 last Tuesday. In the MFT you find the record: SI timestamps all show last Tuesday 03:14, but FN creation shows 2021 — classic timestomping, and itself evidence of malicious intent. The record is marked deleted, yet the filename and timestamps are intact, and the data runs point to clusters you can carve. From this one record you learn: the file existed, when it really arrived (FN birth, corroborated by other artifacts), that someone tried to hide its age, and where its content may still sit on disk. Common mistakes: trusting Explorer timestamps alone (they show SI, the forgeable set); assuming 'deleted' means 'gone' (it means 'marked free'); and analyzing the live disk instead of an image — every write you make risks overwriting the very unallocated clusters holding deleted evidence. Two companion artifacts make MFT analysis far stronger: $LogFile and $UsnJrnl. The NTFS log file ($LogFile) records transactional metadata changes — file creations, deletions, renames — and can reveal activity whose MFT record was later reused. The Update Sequence Number Journal ($UsnJrnl) logs file changes with timestamps and reasons (creation, deletion, rename, data overwrite), giving you a second witness when MFT timestamps look tampered. Together, MFT + $UsnJrnl let you catch timestomping red-handed: the journal says the file was created Tuesday while SI claims 2019. On resident versus non-resident data: small files and alternate data streams may live inside the MFT record itself (resident), which means they survive even when the file's clusters are long overwritten — malware configuration blobs hidden in ADS are recoverable this way. Large files are non-resident: the MFT stores data runs (cluster addresses), and carving follows those runs across the disk. Worked micro-example: an MFT record for invoice.pdf shows SI timestamps of last month but the $UsnJrnl entry for the same file reference number shows creation yesterday with reason 'file create' — the file is new, the timestamps are forged, and the journal entry is your proof. Common tooling note: parse the MFT with a proper parser (many free ones exist) rather than eyeballing hex — the attribute layouts are intricate, and misreading an attribute offset produces confident nonsense. Always work from the image, and always cross-check a surprising MFT finding against at least one other artifact before building conclusions on it.

notes.title: Disk artifacts II: prefetch, event logs, and the registry
notes.body: Three more Windows artifact families answer 'what ran, when, and by whom.' Prefetch: Windows tracks application startup to speed it up, storing a .pf file per executed program in C:\Windows\Prefetch. Each prefetch file records the executable name, a hash of its path, the last run time, and a run count. If malware.exe ran, prefetch usually proves it — including how many times. Windows Event Logs: the Security log records logons (event 4624 successful, 4625 failed), process creation (4688, when auditing is enabled), and account changes; the System log records service installs and shutdowns; PowerShell operational logs can capture script blocks. Registry hives: HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Enum\USBSTOR proves which USB devices were connected (by serial number); Run keys (HKLM/HKCU ...\Run) show persistence; Shimcache/AppCompatCache and Amcache record program execution history going back months. Worked example: did someone plug in a personal USB drive and copy files? USBSTOR shows a SanDisk device serial 4C530001 connected Tuesday 14:02; the Security log shows logon 4624 for the user at 13:58; prefetch shows notepad.exe is irrelevant but a portable file manager ran 14 times with last run 14:20; Amcache corroborates the file manager's first execution at 14:05. Four independent artifacts, one story. Operator gotchas: event logs roll over — on a busy domain controller the Security log may only cover days, so check log size and retention settings during preparation, not during the incident; 4688 process-creation auditing is off by default on many builds, so enable it fleet-wide now via GPO; and always note the system's timezone before interpreting timestamps — a three-hour offset has sunk real investigations. Two more high-value sources complete the Windows artifact picture. Sysmon, when installed, logs process creation with full command lines and hashes, network connections per process, and driver loads — it is the single richest endpoint telemetry source on Windows, and deploying it fleet-wide via GPO is one of the highest-value preparation tasks you can do. Without Sysmon, enable 4688 process-creation auditing with command-line logging as the fallback. Amcache.hve deserves special attention: it records executed programs with their first-execution timestamps, file paths, and SHA-1 hashes, often going back months further than prefetch — when prefetch has rolled over, Amcache frequently still has the answer. For USB investigations, pair USBSTOR with the setupapi.dev.log (device install timestamps) and the Security log to build connection windows. And the preparation lesson that dwarfs all artifact knowledge: centralize your logs before the incident. Windows Event Forwarding (WEF) or a SIEM collecting Security, System, and PowerShell logs means the evidence survives even if the attacker wipes the local logs — which, per ATT&CK T1070.001, is one of the first things intruders do. Size the retention for your event volume: a domain controller generating 50,000 events a day with a 20 MB log keeps roughly hours of history. That sizing math belongs in preparation, decided once, not discovered during triage when the logs you need rolled over yesterday.

notes.title: Memory basics: what lives in RAM and how to grab it
notes.body: RAM holds the live state of the machine: running processes and their full command lines, loaded DLLs, active network connections and sockets, decrypted content (passwords, keys, chat messages that are encrypted on disk), injected or hollowed code that never touches the disk (fileless malware lives here and only here), clipboard contents, and open handles to files and registry keys. That is why memory is captured before anything else on a live system — and why powering off is the most destructive single action an investigator can take. Acquisition means writing RAM contents to a file on external media using a memory acquisition tool, run from that external media, with the output going to the external drive — never to the suspect's own disk. Two partial-memory sources exist when live capture is impossible: pagefile.sys (paged-out memory, partial and unordered) and hiberfil.sys (a compressed RAM snapshot from hibernation — often a goldmine on laptops). After acquisition, analysis tools can list processes, including hidden ones, extract network connections at capture time, and dump suspicious process memory for strings and malware analysis. Worked example: EDR flags credential dumping on a workstation. You arrive, machine on. You photograph the screen, run the acquisition tool from your USB drive writing to the same drive, and in 8 minutes have a 16 GB memory image. Analysis later shows lsass.exe with an unexpected injected thread and a network connection to an external IP — the fileless component that disk forensics alone would never have found. Common mistakes: capturing memory TO the suspect disk (overwrites unallocated space and pagefile evidence); running the tool from the suspect disk (same problem, plus it may be intercepted); and assuming 'the EDR has logs, so memory does not matter' — EDR sees events, memory shows state, and fileless techniques are designed to be invisible to event-only collection. The acquisition workflow in practice: arrive, photograph, then run the memory tool from external media with output directed to the same external media — the command line, tool version, start and end times all go in your notes. Expect roughly one minute per gigabyte on modern hardware; a 16 GB laptop takes 10-20 minutes, during which the machine must stay powered and undisturbed. If the machine is locked, do not attempt to log in as the user (you will change last-logon artifacts and potentially trigger the attacker's awareness); capture memory from the lock screen state — the RAM contents are what matter, not the desktop. Beyond full RAM, know your partial sources: pagefile.sys holds paged-out memory in no particular order — strings carved from it can yield passwords, URLs, and chat fragments months old. hiberfil.sys on laptops is a compressed full-RAM snapshot from the last hibernation — analysts have recovered entire intrusion sessions from it. The swapfile and memory compression stores on newer Windows builds add further fragments. Analysis begins with the basics: process list (look for processes with no name, odd parents, or injected threads), network connections at capture time, and loaded DLLs per process. Then strings analysis on dumped process memory — attacker infrastructure, commands, and stolen data often sit in cleartext. Anti-forensic awareness: sophisticated malware may detect acquisition tools or wipe on shutdown, which is one more reason memory comes before any other action. And the legal note: memory can contain other users' private data (open documents, messages) — handle the image with the same custody and access controls as any sensitive evidence.

notes.title: Timeline analysis: one clock to rule them all
notes.body: Timeline analysis merges timestamps from every artifact source into a single chronological narrative — the 'super-timeline' concept. No single artifact tells the story; the MFT says when a file appeared, prefetch says when it executed, event logs say who was logged on, browser history says what was downloaded, and only together do they describe the intrusion. The method: extract timestamps from each source, normalize them to one timezone (UTC is the standard — record the conversion), sort, and read the story. Deduplicate and sanity-check: a file 'created' after it was 'executed' signals timestomping or clock issues, not time travel. Worked example: reconstructing a phishing compromise. 09:02 — browser history: user downloads invoice.doc from a lookalike domain. 09:14 — MFT: invoice.doc created in Downloads (FN and SI agree — no tampering). 09:15 — prefetch: WINWORD.EXE last run 09:15, run count increments. 09:15 — Security log 4688: powershell.exe spawned with parent winword.exe (the smoking gun). 09:16 — prefetch: powershell.exe first run. 09:22 — Security log 4624: anomalous logon to the file server from this workstation. 09:31 — MFT: new scheduled task XML created. Read top to bottom, that is the entire attack: delivery, execution, privilege action, lateral movement, persistence — each step corroborated by a different artifact family, each timestamp in UTC. Operator gotchas: mixed timezones are the classic timeline killer — Windows event logs are UTC internally but displayed in local time, while some artifacts are local; normalize everything before sorting. And document your sources: a timeline row should always say which artifact produced it, so the story survives scrutiny. Tooling for timelines ranges from manual to automated, and you should understand both. The manual method — spreadsheet, one row per artifact, UTC-normalized — is slow but teaches you what each artifact actually means, which is why this module's lab uses it. The automated method follows the super-timeline concept: tools like Plaso (log2timeline) parse dozens of artifact types into a single sorted bodyfile. Automation is fast and comprehensive, but it is garbage-in-garbage-out: feed it a misconfigured timezone and every row is wrong with great confidence. Whichever method you use, the interpretation discipline is the same: cluster related rows (the five events within 90 seconds of the malicious download are one action, not five mysteries), flag anomalies (timestamps out of order, gaps where logs were cleared), and write the narrative in plain sentences before concluding. Timelines also exonerate: 'the user was accused of exfiltrating data at 3 PM, but the timeline shows their workstation was locked from 1 PM and the transfer came from a service account' — that finding matters as much as any guilty one. Timezone handling in detail: record every source's native timezone assumption (event logs: UTC internally; prefetch: local system time as FILETIME UTC; browser history: varies), convert everything to UTC once, and state the conversion in your report. When the timeline spans multiple machines, verify each machine's clock offset — a workstation five minutes fast can invert cause and effect. A timeline without documented timezone handling is a story, not evidence.

notes.title: Chain of custody and imaging: make your evidence defensible
notes.body: Chain of custody is the documented, unbroken record of who handled evidence, when, and what they did with it. It starts the moment you decide something is evidence: tag it, log the date, time, collector, source system, and a cryptographic hash (SHA-256) of the acquired data. Every subsequent access — analysis, copying, storage moves — gets logged. If custody breaks (an undocumented gap, an unverified copy), the evidence's integrity can be challenged, whether in court, in HR proceedings, or in front of an insurer. The technical foundation is the forensic image: a bit-for-bit copy of the disk, acquired through a write-blocker (hardware or software that prevents any write to the source drive). You then hash the source and the image — matching hashes prove the copy is exact — and you analyze the image, never the original. Free tooling covers the whole workflow: FTK Imager (free from AccessData) creates forensic images and computes hashes; Autopsy (free, open-source) is a full analysis platform for disk images; KAPE and Eric Zimmerman's tools (free) do fast targeted collection of key artifacts; Volatility (free, open-source) analyzes memory images. Worked example: custody log entries for a laptop. '2026-10-08 14:20 — J. Rivera collected Dell Latitude SN XXXXX from desk 12, powered on, photographed screen. 14:28 — RAM captured to USB-03 (16 GB image, SHA-256: 9f2c...). 14:45 — disk imaged via write-blocker to EVIDENCE-01 (SHA-256 source = image: a41d...). Stored in safe, shelf B.' That log, plus the matching hashes, is what makes everything downstream defensible. Common mistakes: analyzing the original disk instead of a copy; imaging without a write-blocker (Windows will happily write to a mounted suspect drive); and collecting evidence with no log at all — undocumented evidence is just data with a story nobody can verify. Custody continues after collection: store images on encrypted media in a locked location with restricted access, log every access (who, when, why), and re-verify hashes whenever the image is copied — a hash checked at collection and never again proves nothing about the copy you analyzed six months later. For incidents that might become HR or legal matters, establish a legal hold early: written instruction to preserve specified evidence, suspending normal retention-deletion for those items, with counsel's involvement. The hold prevents the classic disaster of the backup rotation overwriting the key evidence mid-investigation. Documentation standards that survive scrutiny: contemporaneous notes (written during, not after), exact commands with versions, source identifiers (make, model, serial, asset tag), and hash values recorded in at least two places (your notes and the evidence label). Photograph physical evidence in place before moving it — the sticky note with the password on the monitor is evidence of the user's practice, and its position matters. When transferring evidence, use a handoff log: giver, receiver, date, time, hash verification at transfer. Common failure modes: the 'trusted colleague' handoff with no log ('I gave the drive to Dave'), analyzing from the only copy (always work from a verified duplicate, keeping a pristine master), and storing evidence on a network share with broad access (defense counsel will ask who else could have touched it — 'everyone in IT' is a bad answer). Custody is boring until the day it is the entire case.

notes.title: The reimage checklist: what an IT infrastructure specialist preserves first
notes.body: The moment that defines a junior operator is the compromised workstation that 'just needs to be reimaged.' Reimaging is legitimate eradication — but reimaging before preservation destroys the evidence that explains how the attacker got in, which means the next machine falls the same way. The pre-reimage preservation runbook, in order: (1) Isolate the host from the network (EDR isolation, unplug, or disable Wi-Fi) — leave it powered on. (2) Photograph the screen and note the time, logged-on user, and visible applications. (3) Capture RAM to external media if the machine is on and the situation warrants it (credential theft, fileless malware suspected). (4) Pull the high-value targeted artifacts: Security/System event logs (export as .evtx), prefetch directory listing, Amcache/Shimcache, USBSTOR and Run keys from the registry, the MFT (or better, a full disk image if time and storage allow). (5) Record active network connections and running processes with command lines. (6) Write it all down: what you collected, when, hashes of the images, where they are stored — the start of your chain of custody. (7) Only now: reimage from known-good media (not from the machine's own recovery partition, which may be compromised), rejoin to the domain, restore user data from a clean backup, and reset the user's credentials. Worked example: help desk ticket — 'laptop slow, popups, user clicked a weird link.' The tech isolates, spends 20 minutes pulling RAM, event logs, prefetch, and registry hives to the evidence drive, documents hashes, then reimages from USB media. Analysis later shows the initial access was a fake software update — which leads to blocking that domain fleet-wide and a targeted awareness note. The 20 minutes of preservation turned one cleanup into fleet-wide prevention. Operator gotchas: 'the user needs it back today' pressure is real — the runbook exists so preservation is fast and routine, not a debate; never reimage from the local recovery partition on a compromised host; and tell the user what you are doing and why — 'I am saving diagnostic data before rebuilding' beats a mysterious 20-minute delay. The communication around reimaging matters as much as the technical steps. Tell the user what is happening in plain words: 'Your machine shows signs of compromise, so I am saving diagnostic data before rebuilding it clean — this takes about 20 minutes, then you will have a fresh system.' That single sentence prevents the 'IT took my laptop and will not say why' resentment cycle. Give a realistic return time and keep it; if analysis will take days, say so and provide a loaner. After reimaging, validate before returning: confirm the build came from known-good media (verify the image hash if your process supports it), confirm EDR and patching are active, restore only user data (documents, not executables or installers) from a backup predating the incident, and reset the user's password with MFA re-enrollment. Then close the loop back into detection: the preserved artifacts should produce at least one improvement — a blocked domain, a new detection rule, a GPO change, or an awareness note. The reimage checklist is therefore not the end of the incident but a handoff: preservation → rebuild → return → improve. Track the metric that proves the runbook's value: mean time from 'suspected compromise' to 'preserved and rebuilding.' When leadership asks what the security program delivers, 'we preserve evidence on every suspected host within 30 minutes and every case improves a control' is an answer backed by process, not adjectives. And keep the runbook itself under version control with a review date — the checklist that nobody updates quietly becomes the checklist nobody follows.

cards.front: State the order of volatility from most to least volatile.
cards.back: Registers/cache → RAM → network state → running processes → disk → remote logs → physical config → archival media.

cards.front: A suspect machine is powered on. What is the single most destructive action you can take?
cards.back: Powering it off or rebooting — it destroys RAM contents (processes, connections, keys, fileless malware).

cards.front: MFT: what do the $STANDARD_INFORMATION and $FILE_NAME timestamps tell you?
cards.back: SI is what Explorer shows and is easily forged (timestomping). FN is set at creation and hard to fake — a mismatch between them signals timestamp tampering.

cards.front: What does a Windows prefetch (.pf) file prove?
cards.back: That a program executed: executable name, path hash, last run time, and run count.

cards.front: Which registry key proves a specific USB device was connected, and by what identifier?
cards.back: HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Enum\USBSTOR — by the device's serial number.

cards.front: Security log event IDs for successful logon, failed logon, and process creation?
cards.back: 4624 = successful logon, 4625 = failed logon, 4688 = process creation (requires auditing enabled).

cards.front: Why capture memory to external media instead of the suspect's own disk?
cards.back: Writing to the suspect disk overwrites unallocated space, the pagefile, and deleted-file evidence you are trying to preserve.

cards.front: What is a forensic image and how do you prove it is exact?
cards.back: A bit-for-bit copy of the disk, acquired through a write-blocker. Matching SHA-256 hashes of source and image prove exactness.

cards.front: Name four free forensic tools and what each does.
cards.back: FTK Imager (disk imaging + hashing), Autopsy (disk image analysis platform), KAPE / Eric Zimmerman tools (fast targeted artifact collection), Volatility (memory image analysis).

cards.front: What is timeline (super-timeline) analysis?
cards.back: Merging timestamps from all artifact sources (MFT, logs, prefetch, browser history), normalized to one timezone, into a single chronological narrative of the incident.

cards.front: What starts a chain of custody, and what breaks it?
cards.back: It starts when you log the evidence: date, time, collector, source, and hash. An undocumented gap in handling or an unverified copy breaks it.

cards.front: Before reimaging a suspect workstation, list the preservation order.
cards.back: Isolate (leave powered on) → photograph screen → capture RAM → pull event logs, prefetch, registry hives, MFT/disk image → record connections/processes → document with hashes → then reimage from known-good media.

quiz.q: You arrive at a running workstation flagged for credential dumping. What do you collect FIRST?
choices: RAM contents, to external media
A full disk image
The Windows event logs
The MFT
quiz.explain: RAM is the most volatile evidence that matters here — injected code, LSASS contents, and active connections vanish on shutdown. Disk artifacts persist; memory does not.

quiz.q: An MFT record shows $STANDARD_INFORMATION timestamps from last Tuesday but $FILE_NAME creation from 2021. What does this indicate?
choices: Timestomping — someone forged the SI timestamps
Normal Windows behavior
Disk corruption
The file was copied last Tuesday
quiz.explain: FN creation is set at file creation and hard to modify; SI is easily forged. A large SI/FN discrepancy is the classic timestomping signature — itself evidence of malicious intent.

quiz.q: Prefetch shows evil.exe with a run count of 14 and last run yesterday. What is proven?
choices: The program executed at least 14 times, most recently yesterday
The program is currently running
The program was downloaded yesterday
The program was deleted yesterday
quiz.explain: Prefetch records execution history (name, path hash, last run, count) — it proves execution, not current state, download time, or deletion.

quiz.q: To prove which USB drive was plugged into a workstation, you check:
choices: USBSTOR registry key, matching the device serial number
The Recycle Bin
Browser download history
The pagefile
quiz.explain: Enum\USBSTOR records each connected USB storage device by serial number with install timestamps — the authoritative artifact for 'which drive.'

quiz.q: A colleague suggests rebooting the suspect laptop 'to see if the malware comes back.' Why is this wrong?
choices: Reboot destroys RAM evidence and changes system state before anything was captured
Rebooting is always illegal
Malware cannot survive a reboot
Event logs are wiped on reboot
quiz.explain: The reboot wipes the most volatile evidence (memory) and alters timestamps and state. Capture first, then make controlled changes — and document each one.

quiz.q: You image a suspect drive without a write-blocker by just plugging it into your workstation. What is the risk?
choices: Your OS may write to the drive, altering evidence and breaking hash verification
The image will be too large
NTFS cannot be imaged this way
The hash will compute faster
quiz.explain: Windows writes to mounted volumes (thumbs.db, logs, timestamps). A write-blocker guarantees the source is unaltered so source and image hashes match.

quiz.q: In a super-timeline, a file's MFT 'created' time is AFTER its prefetch 'last run' time. What should you suspect?
choices: Timestomping or a clock/timezone problem — investigate, do not trust the order blindly
The timeline tool is broken; discard it
The file was never executed
Normal behavior for system files
quiz.explain: Execution cannot precede creation. The inconsistency signals forged timestamps or mixed timezones — normalize timezones first, then treat the anomaly as a lead.

quiz.q: Which memory artifact would reveal fileless malware that never wrote to disk?
choices: An injected thread or hollowed process visible in the RAM capture
The MFT record
Prefetch
The Shimcache
quiz.explain: Fileless malware lives only in memory — disk artifacts (MFT, prefetch, Shimcache) may show nothing. Only a memory capture reveals injected code and hollowed processes.

quiz.q: Chain of custody is best described as:
choices: The documented, unbroken record of who handled evidence, when, and what was done — anchored by hashes
The encryption password for the evidence drive
A list of suspects
The backup schedule for evidence storage
quiz.explain: Custody = documentation + hashes at every handoff. It is what makes evidence defensible to management, HR, insurers, or a court.

quiz.q: Before reimaging a compromised workstation, the LAST preservation step is:
choices: Documenting everything collected — what, when, hashes, storage location
Pulling the network cable
Capturing RAM
Exporting event logs
quiz.explain: Documentation closes the preservation phase and opens the custody record. Without it, the collected artifacts are just files with a story nobody can verify.

items.prompt: Most volatile evidence category?
items.answer: CPU registers and cache (then RAM, in practical terms).
items.explain: Volatility order starts with registers/cache — gone in microseconds.

items.prompt: Practical first capture on a live suspect machine?
items.explain: RAM is the most volatile evidence you can actually capture.

items.prompt: Artifact proving a program executed, with run count?
items.explain: Name, path hash, last run time, run count.

items.prompt: Registry key for USB device history?
items.explain: Records devices by serial number.

items.prompt: Event ID for successful logon?
items.explain: 4625 is failed logon; 4688 is process creation.

items.prompt: Hash algorithm commonly used to verify forensic images?
items.explain: Matching source/image hashes prove a bit-exact copy.

items.prompt: Free tool for creating forensic disk images?
items.explain: Free imaging + hashing tool.

items.prompt: Free open-source memory analysis framework?
items.explain: Analyzes RAM captures: processes, connections, injected code.

items.prompt: Suspect laptop is powered OFF on the desk. Do you power it on to look around?
items.answer: No — image the disk first (write-blocked), then analyze the image. Powering on alters evidence.
items.explain: Dead-box rule: the disk is stable evidence; booting it contaminates timestamps and unallocated space.

items.prompt: EDR shows credential dumping but disk scans find no malware file. Where do you look?
items.answer: Memory capture — fileless techniques live only in RAM (injected threads, hollowed processes).
items.explain: Absence of disk artifacts plus credential-theft behavior is the classic fileless pattern.

items.prompt: You need to prove a user ran a portable app from USB last month. Name three artifacts.
items.answer: USBSTOR (device + serial), prefetch or Amcache/Shimcache (execution), Security log 4624 (logon timing).
items.explain: Corroboration across artifact families is what makes the finding solid.

items.prompt: The Security log only covers the last 2 days on a busy server. What preparation failure is this?
items.answer: Log size/retention was never sized for the event volume — and no central log forwarding.
items.explain: Retention is a preparation task; check it before the incident, and forward logs centrally.

items.prompt: You collected a disk image but kept no log of when, by whom, or its hash. What is the consequence?
items.answer: Broken chain of custody — the evidence's integrity cannot be verified or defended.
items.explain: Undocumented evidence is just data with an unverifiable story.

items.prompt: User demands their laptop back today; you have isolated it but not preserved anything. What do you do?
items.answer: Run the 20-minute preservation runbook (RAM, logs, prefetch, registry, hashes, documentation), then reimage from known-good media.
items.explain: The runbook exists to make preservation fast and non-negotiable, not a debate under pressure.

handsOnLab.title: Build a mini-timeline from your own Windows machine
handsOnLab.brief: Using only built-in Windows tools and PowerShell, you will extract real forensic artifacts from your own machine — event logs, prefetch, USB history, Run keys — normalize their timestamps, and assemble a short timeline answering a concrete question. No suspect machine needed; the technique is identical.
steps: Open PowerShell as Administrator on your Windows machine (your own — never practice on someone else's).
Export the last 7 days of the Security log: Get-WinEvent -LogName Security -MaxEvents 500 | Export-Clixml .\sec-log.xml — note the export time in UTC.
Find logon events: parse for IDs 4624/4625 and list the 5 most recent with time, user, and logon type.
List prefetch entries: Get-ChildItem C:\Windows\Prefetch\*.pf | Sort LastWriteTime -Descending | Select Name, LastWriteTime -First 10 — record what ran most recently.
Check USB history: Get-ChildItem 'HKLM:\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Enum\USBSTOR' — list each device subkey (serial numbers) you find.
Check persistence: Get-ItemProperty 'HKCU:\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run' and the HKLM equivalent — list every value.
Convert all timestamps to UTC and build timeline.md: one row per finding with UTC time, artifact source, and what it shows.
Answer in writing: 'When was this machine last logged on, what ran most recently, and has any USB storage device ever been connected?' — citing artifact + timestamp per claim.
Write a 5-line chain-of-custody note for your exports: what you collected, when (UTC), and where the files are stored.
Hash your export files: Get-FileHash .\sec-log.xml -Algorithm SHA256 — record the hash in your custody note.
Identify one gap: which artifact you wanted but could not get (e.g., 4688 disabled, log rolled over) and what preparation change would fix it.
Re-read your timeline as an investigator: does every claim cite a source artifact? Fix any uncited claims.
handsOnLab.deliverable: timeline.md (UTC-normalized findings table + written answers with cited artifacts) and custody-note.txt (collection log + SHA-256 hashes).
handsOnLab.checkpoint: Every factual claim in timeline.md cites a specific artifact and UTC timestamp; the custody note lists each export with its SHA-256 hash; and you have named one logging gap plus its preparation fix.

videos.title: SANS Institute YouTube channel — digital forensics and incident response talks
videos.blurb: The SANS Institute's official channel hosts DFIR webcasts and talks covering memory forensics, timeline analysis, and Windows artifacts at practitioner depth.

mockTask.q: Panel question: A user's laptop is suspected compromised and the help desk wants to reimage it immediately to get the user working again. What do you do?
choices: Isolate the host, run the preservation runbook (RAM, event logs, prefetch, registry hives, hashes, documentation — about 20 minutes), then reimage from known-good media
Reimage immediately — user productivity comes first and the EDR already logged everything
Power the laptop off and reimage it tomorrow when things are calmer
Reimage from the laptop's built-in recovery partition to save time
mockTask.explain: Preservation before reimaging keeps the evidence that reveals the entry point (so the fleet can be protected); EDR logs do not replace memory and artifact evidence; powering off destroys RAM; and a local recovery partition on a compromised host is untrusted.

title: Threat Intelligence & MITRE ATT&CK Mapping
summary: How to think like an adversary and explain it like an operator: indicators of compromise versus indicators of attack, the MITRE ATT&CK knowledge base in plain language, mapping a blocked action to a tactic and technique, and translating blocks into explanations non-technical stakeholders actually understand.
objectives: Distinguish IOCs from IOAs and explain why behavior-based indicators are more durable.
Describe ATT&CK tactics versus techniques in plain language and walk an attack end to end.
Map an observed or blocked action to the correct ATT&CK tactic and technique, including technique ID format.
Explain a security block to executives, end users, and auditors without jargon.
Use ATT&CK coverage mapping to find detection blind spots and prioritize improvements.

notes.title: IOCs vs IOAs: artifacts versus behaviors
notes.body: Threat intelligence speaks in two kinds of indicators. An indicator of compromise (IOC) is a forensic artifact: a file hash, an IP address, a domain name, a filename, a registry key. IOCs are precise and easy to share — you can block a hash in seconds — but they are brittle: the attacker changes the hash with every build, rotates IPs hourly, and registers fresh domains daily.
