An indicator of attack (IOA), also called a behavioral indicator, describes what the attacker DOES: 'a Microsoft Office application spawning a command shell,' 'credential dumping from LSASS memory,' 'a scheduled task created for persistence.' IOAs are harder to write but far more durable — the attacker's tools change weekly, their tactics change yearly. Mature defenses layer both: IOCs for fast blocking of known-bad artifacts, IOAs for catching the behavior even when every artifact is new. Worked example: a ransomware crew hits three companies. Company A shares the payload hash (IOC) — useful for exactly one variant. Company B shares the behavior chain (IOA): phishing document → macro → PowerShell download cradle → credential theft → lateral movement via SMB. Company C, which never saw the hash, still detects the attack because its defenses key on the PowerShell-from-Office behavior. The hash was dead in a day; the behavior is still catching that crew's attacks months later. Common mistakes: building a detection program on IOC feeds alone (you are always one variant behind); treating every IOC as permanent (stale IOCs cause false positives — expire them); and the reverse error — dismissing IOCs entirely (they are cheap, fast, and excellent for triage even if they are not a strategy). Security researcher David Bianco's Pyramid of Pain organizes indicators by how much pain changing them causes the attacker — and it is the best mental model for why IOAs beat IOCs. At the bottom (trivial to change): hashes, IPs, domains. In the middle: network and host artifacts, tools. At the top (painful to change): tactics, techniques, and procedures — the adversary's actual tradecraft. Your detection program should climb the pyramid deliberately: block the easy IOCs automatically, but invest analyst time at the TTP level, because that is where detections survive the attacker's next build. Sharing intelligence follows the same logic. IOCs are shared as simple lists and feeds; richer context travels in structured formats like STIX/TAXII, and frameworks like ATT&CK give both sides a common language so 'we saw T1059.001 from a Word macro' means the same thing to every team. A practical sharing example: after your ransomware case, you publish an internal bulletin with the phishing sender domain (IOC, expires in 30 days), the malicious hash (IOC), and the behavior chain — Office macro → encoded PowerShell → LSASS access → scheduled task (IOAs, kept as detections permanently). The IOCs age out; the behavior detections keep paying. One caution on consuming external intel: every feed contains false positives and stale entries. Before blocking a feed IOC fleet-wide, check age, source confidence, and whether the artifact could be shared infrastructure (a compromised legitimate site is not the same as an attacker domain). Intelligence is evidence to evaluate, not orders to execute.

notes.title: ATT&CK in plain language: tactics are the why, techniques are the how
notes.body: MITRE ATT&CK is a public knowledge base of how real adversaries behave, organized as matrices (Enterprise covers Windows, macOS, Linux, and cloud). Its two core concepts: tactics are the adversary's objectives — the 'why' at each stage (get in, run code, stay in, steal credentials, move around, take data, cause damage). Techniques are the specific methods — the 'how' (spearphishing attachment, PowerShell, scheduled tasks, credential dumping). Each technique has an ID like T1059 (Command and Scripting Interpreter) and sub-techniques like T1059.001 (PowerShell) — the numbering is just an address, not a ranking. Procedures are the specific implementations seen in the wild. The mental model: tactic = chapter heading, technique = section, procedure = the worked example. You do not need to memorize the matrix; you need to be fluent in the ten or so tactics and techniques you will actually encounter on an endpoint fleet, and know how to look up the rest. Worked example: an alert says 'winword.exe launched powershell.exe with an encoded command.' Tactic: Execution (the adversary is trying to run code). Technique: T1059 Command and Scripting Interpreter, sub-technique T1059.001 PowerShell. The procedure — encoded PowerShell from a Word macro — is also a Defense Evasion signal (obfuscation). One observed action, two tactic mappings, one precise technique ID. That is ATT&CK fluency: behavior in, structured language out. Operator gotchas: mapping is analyst judgment, not math — two analysts can map the same event to adjacent techniques, and that is fine as long as you cite the observed behavior; technique IDs change across ATT&CK versions, so always note which version you used; and never present a mapping as certainty to stakeholders — 'consistent with' beats 'this was definitely.' ATT&CK comes in matrices for different domains: Enterprise (Windows, macOS, Linux, cloud, containers — the one you will live in), Mobile, and ICS. Within Enterprise, platforms let you filter techniques to your reality — a Windows fleet cares about a different subset than a cloud-native shop. Navigating the knowledge base is a skill: start from the tactic pages to learn the story, drill into techniques for detection and mitigation guidance (each technique page lists data sources, detection ideas, and mitigations — free consulting from the people who catalogued the adversary), and check the procedure examples to see how real groups implement it. Note the version: ATT&CK updates regularly, techniques get renamed, split, or deprecated, so cite the version in your documentation the way you would cite any reference. A second core concept worth naming: ATT&CK also catalogues mitigations and data sources per technique, which makes it a defensive planning tool, not just an attacker encyclopedia. When your coverage map shows a blind spot on T1053.005 Scheduled Task, the technique page itself tells you which logs to collect and which mitigations apply. Common beginner trap: treating ATT&CK as a compliance checklist ('we must cover all techniques') — it is a knowledge base for prioritization, not a standard to certify against. The goal is risk-informed coverage of the techniques most likely used against your environment, defended in depth, with the reasoning documented. That reasoning — why these techniques, why these controls — is what a panel respects, not the percentage covered.

notes.title: Walking an attack: initial access to impact in plain words
notes.body: ATT&CK tactics roughly follow the order of a real intrusion. Learn them as a story: Reconnaissance (learning about the target) and Resource Development (buying domains, building malware) happen before contact. Initial Access is the break-in — most commonly spearphishing attachment or link, but also valid accounts and exposed services. Execution runs the attacker's code (malicious macros, PowerShell). Persistence makes it survive reboots (scheduled tasks, Run keys, new services). Privilege Escalation gets higher rights. Defense Evasion hides the activity (obfuscation, disabling logging, timestomping). Credential Access steals logins (dumping LSASS, keylogging). Discovery maps the environment (who is admin, what shares exist). Lateral Movement spreads to other machines (SMB, RDP, stolen credentials). Collection gathers the target data. Command and Control maintains the remote channel. Exfiltration sends data out. Impact is the finale — encryption, destruction, or defacement. Worked example — the full walk for a clinic ransomware case: Initial Access: phishing email with 'invoice.doc' (T1566.001 Spearphishing Attachment). Execution: macro launches PowerShell (T1059.001). Persistence: scheduled task 'OfficeUpdate' (T1053.005). Defense Evasion: PowerShell obfuscation, event log clearing (T1070.001). Credential Access: LSASS dump (T1003.001). Discovery: network share enumeration. Lateral Movement: SMB with stolen admin credentials (T1021.004). Impact: data encrypted for ransom (T1486). Notice how one intrusion touches eight tactics — which is why a single well-placed control (blocking Office from spawning shells) disrupts the chain at Execution before the other seven happen. Common mistakes: memorizing IDs without understanding the story (the panel will ask 'walk me through an attack,' not 'recite T-numbers'); treating the tactic order as mandatory (attackers skip, reorder, and loop — cloud attacks may start at Valid Accounts); and mapping only the finale (Impact) while ignoring the six earlier tactics where detection was possible. A second walkthrough cements the pattern — this time a cloud-flavored intrusion, to show the tactics travel. Initial Access: valid credentials bought from an infostealer log (T1078 Valid Accounts) — no phishing needed. Execution: the attacker runs commands through the cloud provider's own management console. Persistence: a new federated identity provider trust (cloud equivalent of a scheduled task). Defense Evasion: deleting cloud audit logs. Credential Access: dumping the identity store. Discovery: enumerating storage buckets and roles. Lateral Movement: assuming roles across accounts. Collection and Exfiltration: copying snapshots to an external account. Impact: deleting the originals. Same tactic story, different techniques — which is exactly why tactic-level thinking transfers across environments while technique specifics change. From the defender's chair, each tactic suggests a control family: Initial Access → phishing-resistant MFA and conditional access; Execution → application control; Persistence → change monitoring on startup mechanisms; Credential Access → credential guarding and tiered admin; Lateral Movement → segmentation; Exfiltration → egress monitoring and data classification. Work that mapping for your own environment once, and you have a security architecture justified in adversary language rather than vendor language. The interview version of this walkthrough takes 90 seconds: pick the endpoint ransomware chain, name each tactic as you go, and land on the punchline — 'and that is why blocking at Execution, before persistence and credential access, is the highest-leverage control we have.' Brevity with structure signals mastery; rambling through fourteen tactics signals memorization.

notes.title: Mapping a blocked action to ATT&CK: the operator's translation
notes.body: When an endpoint control blocks something, your job is to translate the block into adversary language: what tactic was this, what technique, and how confident am I. The method has four steps. (1) Record the raw facts exactly: parent process, child process, command line, user, time, file hashes — no interpretation yet. (2) Ask what the behavior accomplishes for an attacker: running code? staying persistent? stealing credentials? (3) Find the matching tactic and technique in ATT&CK, citing the observed behavior as your evidence. (4) State confidence and alternatives: could this be legitimate admin activity? What would confirm or rule that out? Worked example: the console shows 'Blocked: excel.exe attempted to launch cmd.exe /c powershell -enc <base64>.' Step 1 — facts recorded. Step 2 — an Office app spawning an encoded shell is code execution plus obfuscation. Step 3 — mapping: Execution → T1059 Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059.001 PowerShell); Defense Evasion → T1027 Obfuscated Files or Information (the -enc flag). Step 4 — confidence: high for malicious — no legitimate Excel workflow launches encoded PowerShell; confirmation step: check whether the user opened an emailed workbook in the last hour. Second worked example: 'Blocked: powershell.exe attempted to access LSASS process memory.' Mapping: Credential Access → T1003.001 LSASS Memory. Confidence: high — almost nothing legitimate touches LSASS memory; EDR and AV are the rare exceptions, and they do not do it from powershell.exe. Operator gotchas: do not map from the alert title alone — read the process tree and command line first, because 'PowerShell blocked' could be Execution, Persistence setup, or Discovery depending on what it was doing; record the ATT&CK version with your mapping; and keep a personal mapping journal — after fifty mappings you will be fluent, and the journal is interview gold. Calibrate confidence explicitly, because stakeholders act on your certainty. Three levels work in practice. High: the behavior has almost no legitimate explanation — encoded PowerShell spawned by Word, LSASS accessed from an unsigned binary. Say so, and act. Medium: suspicious but plausibly legitimate — PowerShell downloading a file could be an admin script or a download cradle; confirm with the user or the change record before declaring. Low: consistent with attacker behavior but equally consistent with normal operations — a new scheduled task might be software updater or persistence; investigate, do not alarm. Write the confidence into the ticket alongside the mapping: 'T1059.001, high confidence — no legitimate workflow on this host spawns encoded PowerShell from Office.' That one line lets the next analyst, the manager, and the auditor all move at the right speed. Then turn mappings into detections: every confirmed malicious mapping is a candidate for a permanent rule. The Word-spawns-PowerShell mapping becomes 'alert on any Office application spawning a script interpreter, fleet-wide' — an IOA-based detection born from one incident, protecting against every future variant. Keep a mapping journal as suggested, but review it quarterly: patterns in your mappings reveal your environment's real threat profile. If 80% of your mappings are Initial Access via phishing and Execution via macros, your security roadmap writes itself — email controls, application control, user reporting — and you can defend the budget with your own data instead of industry fear statistics.

notes.title: Explaining blocks to non-technical stakeholders
notes.body: A block explained badly sounds like IT breaking things; explained well, it sounds like the security team doing its job. The translation formula: what happened in plain words, what the attacker was trying to do, what would have happened without the block, and what the person should do — in that order, no jargon, no technique IDs unless asked. Executives care about risk and business impact; end users care about what they did wrong and how to work safely; auditors care about control effectiveness and evidence. Worked example — the same block, three audiences. The block: Excel tried to launch encoded PowerShell, stopped by application control. To the executive: 'This morning we stopped an attack on one workstation. A malicious spreadsheet tried to run a hidden program — the standard first step of a ransomware attack. The workstation is safe, no data was affected, and we are checking whether the same email reached anyone else. No action needed from you.' To the end user: 'The spreadsheet you opened tried to run a hidden program in the background, which is how ransomware gets in — so we blocked it. You did the right thing by reporting the odd email. Please delete it and do not re-open it; if you need the invoice data, ask the sender to resend it as a PDF.' To the auditor: 'Control AC-7 (application allowlisting with script-interpreter containment) blocked T1059.001 execution from a spearphishing attachment at 09:15 on WS-042. EDR telemetry retained; user retraining assigned; IOCs shared.' Same facts, three languages. Common mistakes: leading with the technique ID to an executive (you sound like you are showing off, and they stop listening); blaming the user (they are your detection sensor — praise the report); and overclaiming ('we stopped a nation-state attack' — you stopped a behavior; describe what you observed). Timing and restraint are part of stakeholder communication. Tell executives early but briefly — 'we detected and blocked an attack attempt on one workstation at 09:15; no data affected; investigation underway; next update at noon' — because they should never learn about security events from rumors. Tell users what affects them and what to do, nothing more; a clinic-wide 'we had a cyber incident' email teaches everyone to ignore future messages and occasionally tips off the insider you have not found yet. Tell auditors and compliance with precision and timestamps after the facts are firm. And know what not to say: never speculate about attribution ('it looks Russian') — you almost certainly do not know, and the speculation will be quoted. Never promise 'no data was exfiltrated' until the investigation supports it — say 'no evidence of exfiltration to date; investigation continues.' Never discuss the incident on social media or with reporters unless you are the designated communications lead with a prepared statement. A worked micro-example of restraint done right: the help desk asks 'was it ransomware?' in the ticket thread. Accurate answer: 'We blocked a malicious document attempting code execution — consistent with the early stage of ransomware chains. No encryption occurred. Scoping in progress.' That sentence is truthful, appropriately alarming, and contains zero speculation. Common failure: the analyst who briefs the executive with technique IDs and log excerpts — watch the eyes glaze over, then watch trust erode. Translate, then offer the technical appendix for anyone who wants depth. Communication is a control: it determines whether the organization responds as a team or as a rumor mill.

notes.title: Coverage mapping: finding your blind spots with ATT&CK
notes.body: A coverage map lists the ATT&CK techniques relevant to your environment and marks which ones you can detect, which you can prevent, and which are blind — then prioritizes the blind spots by likelihood and impact. This turns 'we need better security' into an engineering plan. The method: (1) scope to your reality — an endpoint fleet cares most about Initial Access (phishing), Execution, Persistence, Privilege Escalation, Defense Evasion, Credential Access, Lateral Movement, and Impact; (2) for each technique, record your control: prevent (blocked by policy), detect (alerts in the console), or blind (no visibility); (3) prioritize blind spots that are both likely (phishing-delivered execution is extremely common) and high-impact (credential access enables everything downstream). Worked example — a small clinic's map excerpt: T1566.001 Spearphishing Attachment → detect (email gateway + user reports), blind on execution confirmation → priority: enable 4688 process-creation logging. T1059.001 PowerShell → prevent (application control blocks Office-spawned shells) → strong. T1003.001 LSASS Memory → detect (EDR alert) → adequate. T1053.005 Scheduled Task → blind (no monitoring of task creation) → priority: enable 4698 scheduled-task auditing via GPO. T1021.004 SMB lateral movement → blind → priority: segment the network, alert on workstation-to-workstation SMB. Four rows, and you now have a quarter's worth of prioritized projects, each justified in adversary language. Operator gotchas: a map is a living document — update it when you add controls or when ATT&CK versions change; 'detect' without a tested alert is blind with extra steps (tune and test); and start with the techniques attackers actually use against organizations like yours, not the exotic ones — coverage of the common beats coverage of the clever. Presenting the coverage map to leadership is where the exercise pays for itself. One page, three colors: green (prevent), yellow (detect), red (blind) across the techniques most relevant to your environment. Executives do not need all fourteen tactics — show the eight that matter for an endpoint fleet and the story they tell: 'We prevent the common execution techniques, we detect credential theft, but we are blind to persistence mechanisms and lateral movement — here is what each blind spot costs us and what closes it.' Attach a cost and a timeline to each fix: 'Enable scheduled-task auditing via GPO: zero license cost, two weeks, closes persistence blindness.' That framing turns the map into a funded roadmap. Score the map quarterly and trend it — 'blind techniques down from 9 to 4 this year' is a security program metric leadership understands. Link each improvement back to incidents and near-misses: 'This detection would have caught the March phishing attempt at the execution stage instead of the encryption stage.' And keep the map honest about 'detect': a technique is only yellow if the alert exists, is tuned, routes to someone, and has been tested — untested detections are red with better marketing. The final maturity step: use the map for tabletop design. Your blind spots are your scenario injects — 'the attack uses scheduled-task persistence, which we cannot currently see; how do we respond?' — which closes the loop between assessment, exercise, and improvement in one continuous motion.

notes.title: Talking ATT&CK in the ThreatLocker interview
notes.body: The panel does not need you to recite the matrix — they need to see operator fluency: behavior in, structured reasoning out, stakeholder translation on demand. Expect prompts like 'a user is angry we blocked their macro — walk us through it' or 'how would you explain ringfencing to a clinic manager.' The winning structure: state the observed behavior precisely, map it to tactic and technique with the reasoning out loud ('Excel spawning an encoded shell is Execution via T1059.001, with obfuscation suggesting Defense Evasion'), explain why the control fired in adversary terms ('this is the exact step ransomware uses between the phishing email and encryption — blocking here kills the chain before lateral movement'), and close with the stakeholder translation ('so to the user I would say...'). A second high-value move: explain why default-deny controls are ATT&CK-efficient — one policy ('Office apps cannot spawn script interpreters') simultaneously frustrates Execution, Persistence setup, and parts of Defense Evasion across dozens of techniques, whereas IOC blocking plays whack-a-mole with one hash at a time. That single insight demonstrates you think in behaviors, not artifacts. Worked example — panel prompt: 'Why did we block PowerShell for this user?' Strong answer: 'The block fired because winword.exe launched powershell.exe with an encoded command — that maps to Execution, technique T1059.001, and the encoding suggests Defense Evasion. In plain terms: the document tried to run a hidden program, which is step two of nearly every ransomware chain after the phishing email. We stopped it before it could establish persistence or touch credentials. I checked the email source, confirmed it was not a legitimate workflow, and explained to the user what to watch for.' Calm, structured, no jargon overload, ends with the human. Common mistakes: name-dropping technique IDs without explaining the behavior (fluency is reasoning, not vocabulary); freezing when you cannot recall an ID (say 'I would look up the exact sub-technique — the tactic is Execution' — honesty beats bluffing); and badmouthing the user ('they clicked a phish' — the user is the customer). Tie ATT&CK fluency to STAR stories from your own experience, because the panel hires on evidence, not vocabulary. 'Tell me about a time you handled a security alert' becomes: Situation — 'EDR flagged encoded PowerShell from Word on a workstation.' Task — 'Determine if it was malicious and scope it.' Action — 'I mapped it to Execution T1059.001 with Defense Evasion indicators, checked the delivering email, found it reached twelve inboxes, and had IT purge it while I verified no other host executed it.' Result — 'One host reimaged, zero spread, and I wrote the detection rule that now alerts on any Office-spawned interpreter fleet-wide.' Eighty seconds, behavior to mapping to outcome to improvement — that is the whole module in one answer. Prepare three such stories (a block you investigated, a mapping that found a blind spot, a stakeholder explanation that worked) and you can answer most technical-behavioral questions by reaching for one. Also prepare two questions for THEM that show operator thinking: 'How does the team currently map detections to ATT&CK — is there a coverage map I would contribute to?' and 'What does the escalation path look like when a block might be a false positive affecting clinical operations?' Questions like these signal you think about their real problems, not just your interview performance. Final trap to avoid: never inflate. If your ATT&CK experience is this course plus lab work, say so proudly — 'I have mapped fifty scenarios in training and built coverage maps for a fictional clinic; I am fluent in the workflow and honest about the boundary of my experience.' Panels can smell bluffing; they reward the candidate who knows exactly what they know.

cards.front: IOC vs. IOA — define each with an example.
cards.back: IOC = artifact: a file hash, IP, or domain (brittle, changes fast). IOA = behavior: 'Office app spawning a shell' (durable — tactics change slowly).

cards.front: In ATT&CK, what is the difference between a tactic and a technique?
cards.back: Tactic = the adversary's objective, the 'why' (e.g., Execution). Technique = the specific method, the 'how' (e.g., T1059 Command and Scripting Interpreter).

cards.front: What does an ATT&CK technique ID like T1059.001 mean?
cards.back: T1059 is the technique (Command and Scripting Interpreter); .001 is the sub-technique (PowerShell). The number is an address, not a ranking.

cards.front: Excel launches encoded PowerShell. Tactic and technique?
cards.back: Execution → T1059.001 (PowerShell); the encoding also suggests Defense Evasion (T1027 Obfuscation).

cards.front: PowerShell touches LSASS process memory. Tactic and technique?
cards.back: Credential Access → T1003.001 (LSASS Memory).

cards.front: A phishing attachment delivers the first malicious code. Tactic and technique?
cards.back: Initial Access → T1566.001 (Spearphishing Attachment).

cards.front: Data encrypted for ransom. Tactic and technique?
cards.back: Impact → T1486 (Data Encrypted for Impact).

cards.front: Why are IOAs more durable than IOCs for detection?
cards.back: Attackers rotate hashes, IPs, and domains constantly, but reuse the same tactics and techniques for years — behavior outlives artifacts.

cards.front: What is an ATT&CK coverage map?
cards.back: A table of relevant techniques marked prevent / detect / blind, used to prioritize closing the highest-likelihood, highest-impact blind spots.

cards.front: When explaining a block to an executive, what four things do you cover, in order?
cards.back: What happened (plain words) → what the attacker was trying to do → what would have happened without the block → what they should do. No jargon.

cards.front: Why is a default-deny application control 'ATT&CK-efficient'?
cards.back: One policy ('Office apps cannot spawn shells') frustrates Execution, Persistence, and Defense Evasion across dozens of techniques at once — versus blocking one IOC at a time.

cards.front: You cannot recall a technique ID in the interview. What do you do?
cards.back: Say the tactic and reasoning out loud and note you would look up the exact sub-technique — honesty and structured thinking beat bluffing.

quiz.q: Which is an IOA (behavioral indicator) rather than an IOC?
choices: A Word document spawning an encoded PowerShell process
The SHA-256 hash of the malicious document
The IP address of the attacker's server
The domain the malware contacted
quiz.explain: The IOA describes behavior — what the attacker does — which survives hash, IP, and domain rotation. The other three are artifacts (IOCs): precise but brittle.

quiz.q: T1059.001 refers to:
choices: Technique T1059 (Command and Scripting Interpreter), sub-technique PowerShell
Tactic 1059, technique 001
The 1,059,001st recorded attack
A CVE identifier
quiz.explain: ATT&CK IDs are hierarchical addresses: T1059 is the technique, .001 the PowerShell sub-technique. They carry no ranking or severity meaning.

quiz.q: An attacker clears Windows event logs after gaining access. Tactic and technique?
choices: Defense Evasion → T1070.001 (Clear Windows Event Logs)
Impact → T1486
Execution → T1059
Credential Access → T1003
quiz.explain: Deleting evidence of the intrusion is hiding activity — Defense Evasion. The technique is Indicator Removal, sub-technique Clear Windows Event Logs.

quiz.q: Why should IOCs be expired rather than kept forever?
choices: Stale IOCs (reused IPs/domains) cause false positives and alert fatigue
IOCs take up too much disk space
Attackers can sue over old IOCs
Firewalls cannot handle large blocklists
quiz.explain: IPs and domains get reassigned to legitimate owners. Blocking them forever eventually blocks innocent traffic — the classic cost of IOC-only defense.

quiz.q: A new scheduled task named 'OfficeUpdate' runs malware at logon. Tactic and technique?
choices: Persistence → T1053.005 (Scheduled Task)
Initial Access → T1566
Exfiltration → T1041
Discovery → T1083
quiz.explain: Surviving reboot via a scheduled task is the textbook Persistence technique — one of the first things to hunt for on a compromised host.

quiz.q: In a coverage map, 'T1021.004 SMB lateral movement → blind' should be prioritized because:
choices: Lateral movement turns one compromised host into a fleet-wide incident — high likelihood, high impact
SMB is an outdated protocol
It is the easiest to fix
Auditors ask about it most
quiz.explain: Prioritize blind spots by likelihood × impact. Workstation-to-workstation SMB is both common in ransomware spread and catastrophic in effect — network segmentation and alerting belong high on the list.

quiz.q: When mapping a block to ATT&CK, what is the correct FIRST step?
choices: Record the raw facts exactly — processes, command line, user, time — before interpreting
Guess the APT group responsible
Pick the technique ID that sounds closest
Notify the executive team
quiz.explain: Mapping is evidence-driven: facts first, then 'what does this accomplish for an attacker,' then the tactic/technique, then confidence and alternatives. Interpretation before facts produces confident-sounding wrong answers.

quiz.q: An end user asks why their spreadsheet was blocked. The best response:
choices: Explain in plain words that it tried to run a hidden program (a ransomware step), praise their report, and tell them what to do next
Recite the ATT&CK technique IDs involved
Tell them they clicked a phishing email and caused an incident
Say 'security policy' and end the conversation
quiz.explain: Users are your detection sensors — plain language, no blame, clear next steps. Jargon alienates them and blame teaches them to hide the next incident.

quiz.q: Which statement about ATT&CK tactic order is TRUE?
choices: Tactics roughly follow an intrusion's flow, but attackers skip, reorder, and loop — it is not a mandatory sequence
Every attack uses every tactic in order
Impact always comes last and is always ransomware
Initial Access is always phishing
quiz.explain: The tactic list is a story framework, not a checklist. Cloud attacks may start at Valid Accounts; some intrusions never touch certain tactics. Fluency means knowing the story, not enforcing the order.

quiz.q: Two analysts map the same blocked event to slightly different techniques. This is:
choices: Normal — mapping is analyst judgment; what matters is citing the observed behavior as evidence
Proof one of them is incompetent
A sign the event was a false positive
Impossible if they both read ATT&CK
quiz.explain: Adjacent techniques genuinely overlap (is encoded PowerShell Execution or Defense Evasion? — it is both). Defensible mapping cites behavior; reasonable analysts can differ on the label.

items.prompt: IOC or IOA: file hash 5f4dcc3b...?
items.explain: A hash is an artifact — precise but brittle.

items.prompt: IOC or IOA: 'rundll32.exe launching from a Word macro'?
items.explain: A behavior — durable across tool changes.

items.prompt: Tactic for running the attacker's code?
items.explain: The 'why' is running code; T1059 is one 'how.'

items.prompt: Tactic for stealing passwords?
items.explain: E.g., T1003.001 LSASS Memory.

items.prompt: Tactic for spreading host to host?
items.explain: E.g., T1021.004 via SMB with stolen credentials.

items.prompt: Tactic for encrypting data for ransom?
items.explain: T1486 Data Encrypted for Impact.

items.prompt: Tactic for hiding activity, e.g., clearing logs?
items.explain: E.g., T1070.001 Clear Windows Event Logs.

items.prompt: Tactic for the initial phishing email?
items.explain: E.g., T1566.001 Spearphishing Attachment.

items.prompt: Block: 'mshta.exe spawned by outlook.exe'. Map it and state confidence.
items.answer: Execution → T1218.011 (System Binary Proxy Execution: Mshta); high confidence — no legitimate Outlook workflow spawns mshta.
items.explain: Abusing a signed system binary to run code is proxy execution; the parent/child pair is the evidence.

items.prompt: Block: 'vssadmin.exe delete shadows'. Map it.
items.answer: Impact → T1490 (Inhibit System Recovery) — deleting shadow copies precedes ransomware encryption.
items.explain: Killing backups before encrypting is the classic ransomware setup step; treat as pre-Impact warning.

items.prompt: The clinic director asks: 'Are we under attack by a foreign government?' after one blocked macro. Answer?
items.answer: 'We blocked a common attack step — a malicious document trying to run hidden code. We see this pattern constantly; there is no sign of a targeted campaign. Here is what we did and what happens next.'
items.explain: Honest, calming, evidence-bound: describe what you observed, not the scariest possible attribution.

items.prompt: Your coverage map shows 'Scheduled Task creation → blind.' What is the concrete fix?
items.answer: Enable 4698 (scheduled task created) auditing via GPO and build an alert for tasks created outside change windows.
items.explain: Coverage gaps become engineering tasks: a specific log, a specific policy, a specific alert.

items.prompt: A colleague says 'we blocked the hash, incident closed.' What is missing?
items.answer: Behavior-level follow-up: how did it arrive, did it execute anywhere else, is the entry point closed — IOC blocking alone leaves the campaign alive.
items.explain: IOCs stop the artifact; only IOA-level scoping stops the intrusion.

items.prompt: Panel: 'Explain ringfencing to a clinic manager using ATT&CK thinking.' Give the 30-second version.
items.answer: 'Attackers break in with an email, then abuse trusted programs like Word to run their code — that is the Execution step. Ringfencing means Word is allowed to be Word, but never allowed to launch other programs. So even if a malicious document opens, the attack dies at step two instead of spreading.'
items.explain: Behavior → control → outcome, in plain words, ending with why it matters to them.

handsOnLab.title: Map five blocks to ATT&CK and brief three stakeholders
handsOnLab.brief: You will take five realistic blocked-action scenarios, map each to ATT&CK tactic and technique with written reasoning, build a mini coverage map, and write stakeholder explanations — the exact translation skill the ThreatLocker panel tests.
steps: Open the MITRE ATT&CK website (attack.mitre.org) and note the Enterprise matrix version number for your records.
For scenario 1 — 'winword.exe launched powershell.exe -enc <base64>': record raw facts, then map tactic(s), technique ID(s), and confidence with one sentence of reasoning.
Scenario 2 — 'powershell.exe accessed LSASS memory': map and note why confidence differs from scenario 1.
Scenario 3 — 'vssadmin.exe delete shadows /all': map, and write what you would hunt for next (what usually follows this step).
Scenario 4 — 'rundll32.exe with no command line spawned by a browser download': map and list two benign explanations you must rule out.
Scenario 5 — 'a new service installed at 3 AM from a temp directory': map and describe the persistence implication.
Build coverage-map.md: a table with columns technique | scenario | prevent/detect/blind | next improvement.
Mark your blind spots honestly — at least two rows should be 'blind' with a concrete fix (log to enable, policy to write).
Write three stakeholder briefs for scenario 1: a 4-sentence executive brief, a 4-sentence end-user message, and a 3-bullet auditor note.
Read each brief aloud: if any sentence needs a glossary, rewrite it in plain words.
Add a 'mapping journal' entry: which mapping was hardest and what behavior evidence decided it.
Self-review: does every mapping cite observed behavior (not just the alert title)? Fix any that do not.
handsOnLab.deliverable: attack-mapping.md — five mapped scenarios with reasoning and confidence, a coverage table with blind spots and fixes, and three stakeholder briefs for scenario 1.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: Every mapping cites specific observed behavior, technique IDs include sub-techniques where applicable, the coverage table has at least two honest 'blind' rows with concrete fixes, and the stakeholder briefs contain zero unexplained jargon.

videos.title: MITRE official YouTube channel — ATT&CK explainers and technique talks
videos.blurb: MITRE's official channel publishes ATT&CK framework explainers and conference talks on adversary tactics and techniques from the team that maintains the knowledge base.

mockTask.q: Panel question: A user is angry that we blocked the macro in their spreadsheet. Walk us through how you explain the block.
choices: State the observed behavior, map it aloud (Excel spawning an encoded shell = Execution T1059.001, likely Defense Evasion), explain this is the step ransomware uses right after the phishing email, and translate for the user: what happened, why it was blocked, what to do next — no blame
Quote the ATT&CK technique IDs and tell the user to read the matrix
Tell the user macros are against policy and close the ticket
Unblock the macro to keep the user happy and note the exception
mockTask.explain: The panel wants the full operator loop: precise behavior, structured ATT&CK reasoning out loud, adversary-context for why the control fired, and a blameless plain-language user explanation. Quoting IDs without translation, policy-stonewalling, or unblocking a high-confidence malicious behavior all fail.

title: Security Awareness & Social Engineering Defense
summary: How social engineering actually works — phishing, vishing, smishing, pretexting, baiting, tailgating — and how to teach people to resist it. You will build a complete 30-minute awareness session with a handout and attendee quiz, and learn to measure improvement honestly instead of gaming the click rate.
objectives: Dissect a phishing email, a vishing call, and a pretexting scenario to name the manipulation techniques used.
Explain the psychological levers attackers rent: authority, urgency, scarcity, social proof, reciprocity, curiosity.
Design a 30-minute security awareness session with a hook, live demo, habits, practice, and close.
Teach verification habits and build a blameless reporting culture.
Measure awareness with honest baselines: click rate, reporting rate, and repeat-clicker coaching.

notes.title: Phishing anatomy: dissecting the fake invoice
notes.body: Phishing is a crafted lie delivered at scale, and every phish has the same anatomy: a spoofed or lookalike sender, a subject engineered for emotion, a pretext that explains why you are being contacted, a call to action (click, reply, open), and a payload (credential-harvesting page, malicious attachment, or simply a conversation that leads to a wire transfer). Learn to dissect each layer. Sender: display-name spoofing ('Acme Billing <billing@acme-secure-pay.com>') exploits the fact that most people read the display name, not the address; lookalike domains swap characters (acme-biIIing.com with capital i's, or acrnе.com with a Cyrillic e). Headers (in the full message source) reveal the true return path and authentication results. Body: urgency ('your account will be suspended in 24 hours'), authority (a fake CEO, a vendor, IT), and specificity stolen from public sources (your real invoice number from a breached vendor). Links: hover to reveal the true destination — credential phish hides behind 'View Invoice' buttons pointing at unrelated domains. Attachments: Office documents with macros, HTML attachments that render a fake login page locally. Worked example — dissecting a fictional phish line by line: Subject 'ACTION REQUIRED: Past-due invoice #INV-88412.' From: 'Acme Corp Billing <billing@acme-billlng.com>' — note the double-l, lookalike domain. Body thanks you for your business and warns service suspension Friday — urgency plus a real-sounding invoice number. The 'Pay Now' button links to acme-billing-portal.ru — country mismatch, unrelated domain. Attachment 'invoice_88412.html' — an HTML attachment is itself a red flag; opened locally it shows a pixel-perfect Microsoft login asking for credentials. Verdict in one minute: lookalike sender domain, urgency, mismatched link, HTML attachment — four independent red flags. Common mistakes: judging by logos and polish (attackers copy branding perfectly); trusting the display name; and forwarding the phish to a colleague to ask 'is this real?' — which spreads it. Report it through the reporting channel instead. Three phishing variants deserve names because they change the defense. Spearphishing targets a specific person with researched detail — the invoice from your actual vendor, the email from your actual manager (possibly from their compromised account). Whaling targets executives with authority-flavored lures — the fake board memo, the 'urgent acquisition' wire request. Business email compromise (BEC) often has no payload at all — just a conversation: 'Are you available? I need a favor,' followed by gift-card or wire instructions. BEC defeats every attachment scanner ever built because there is nothing malicious to scan — the defense is purely procedural (verify out-of-band, require dual authorization for payments). A newer variant: QR-code phishing ('quishing') — the malicious link hides inside a QR code the email scanner cannot easily read, and the victim scans it with a phone that may lack the company's email protections. Defenses adapt: QR codes in email get the same suspicion as links, and phones get the reporting habit too. Attachment discipline in plain terms: treat unexpected attachments as guilty until verified — Office macros, HTML attachments, ISO/ZIP containers, and especially multi-stage 'open the HTML, click the link, enter credentials' chains. Worked micro-example of BEC defended: the CFO's 'urgent wire' email arrives Friday at 4:55 PM. Procedure: no wire moves on email instruction alone — the finance staffer calls the CFO on the known number. Ninety seconds, attack dead. That procedure, written down and followed under pressure, is worth more than any email filter against BEC.

notes.title: Vishing and smishing: the human firewall under voice pressure
notes.body: Vishing (voice phishing) and smishing (SMS phishing) move the con to channels where people have fewer defenses — no hover-to-inspect on a phone call, and text messages carry an intimacy that email lost a decade ago. The classic vishing script is the fake IT helpdesk: 'Hi, this is Mike from IT, we are seeing suspicious logins on your account, I need to verify your identity — can you read me the code that just arrived on your phone?' Every element is engineered: authority (IT), urgency (suspicious logins), and a request that sounds like verification but is actually the attacker completing a login as you with the MFA code you just read aloud. MFA fatigue attacks (push bombing) spam your phone with approval prompts at 2 AM until you tap approve just to make it stop. Smishing lures impersonate package delivery ('your parcel is held — confirm address'), banks ('unusual transaction — reply YES'), and toll agencies — always with a link to a lookalike site or a callback number the attacker controls. Caller ID is spoofable, so 'the number matched the bank' proves nothing. Worked example — annotated vishing transcript: Caller: 'This is Daniel from IT security, employee ID 4421.' (Red flag 1: unsolicited authority claim — real IT does not cold-call for credentials; employee IDs are theater.) 'We detected your account logging in from Russia.' (Red flag 2: fear + urgency.) 'I am going to send a verification code — read it back so I know it is really you.' (Red flag 3: the inversion — a legitimate verifier never asks you to prove yourself by surrendering a secret; the code is YOUR authentication, and reading it hands over your session.) Correct response, rehearsed: 'I will call the help desk back on the internal number and open a ticket.' Then hang up. Defense in depth: publish the rule 'IT will never ask for your password or MFA code, ever' — a simple, absolute, testable policy — and give people the internal callback number on a card. Common mistakes: debating the caller (engagement is the trap — hang up); calling back the number they gave you (it rings the attacker); and assuming older or non-technical staff are the only targets (executives get whaling calls; IT staff get 'vendor support' calls). Two emerging twists raise the stakes on voice and SMS fraud. AI voice cloning lets an attacker reproduce a trusted voice — a manager, a family member — from seconds of public audio, turning 'verify the voice' from a defense into a vulnerability. The countermeasure is a shared secret or callback procedure agreed in advance: 'any unusual request gets verified by calling back on the known number, no matter how real the voice sounds.' Families use a code word; companies use the callback rule. SIM swapping is the heavier variant: the attacker convinces the carrier to move your number to their SIM, intercepting calls and SMS codes — which is why SMS-based MFA is the weakest form and app-based or hardware MFA is the upgrade path worth pushing. On smishing, the current lure catalog: package delivery ('customs fee due'), toll and DMV notices, bank fraud alerts, and 'wrong number' conversation starters that build rapport over days before the ask (pig-butchering style). The defense pattern never changes: the message supplies urgency and contact details; you supply independent verification. Organization-level defenses: publish the absolute rules ('IT never asks for codes,' 'the bank never texts links'), put the real contact numbers where people can find them in the moment (intranet banner, wallet card, lock-screen wallpaper for shared devices), and run a vishing drill the way you run phishing simulations — a scripted fake IT call to a sample of staff, with kind debriefing. People who have heard the script once recognize it forever; people who have only read about it often do not.

notes.title: Pretexting, baiting, and tailgating: attacks that skip email
notes.body: Not every con arrives as a message. Pretexting is a fabricated scenario used to extract information or access: the 'auditor' who needs the Wi-Fi password for their inspection, the 'vendor technician' here to service the copier who needs a network drop, the caller doing a 'customer satisfaction survey' who walks the receptionist into confirming employee names, titles, and email formats — each answer a building block for the next attack. Baiting dangles something the victim wants: USB drives labeled 'Q3 bonuses' left in the parking lot (when plugged in, they run malware or simply phone home to prove the point), or a 'free software crack' download that is pure trojan. Tailgating (piggybacking) is physical: following an employee through a badge-controlled door with arms full of boxes and a friendly smile — no exploit kit required. The defense is procedural, not technical: a verification habit ('I verify unexpected requests through a known channel'), a challenge culture for physical access ('I do not hold the door — everyone badges in, no exceptions, and that rule protects you too'), and clean-desk / clean-USB policies with the reasoning explained. Worked example — the auditor pretext, defended: A well-dressed visitor tells the front desk she is from the 'state inspection office' and needs the guest Wi-Fi password plus a look at the server room. Trained response: 'I would be glad to help — let me verify your visit with our office manager, who schedules all inspections.' The verification goes through the known internal channel, not the phone number on her business card. If legitimate, the five-minute check costs nothing; if not, it just stopped a physical intrusion. Common mistakes: treating politeness as a security control ('he seemed nice'); verifying through attacker-supplied contact details (the card, the callback number, the email in the signature — all attacker-controlled); and assuming physical attacks are rare — for targeted intrusions they are a standard opening move. Elicitation — the conversational side of pretexting — deserves its own study because it targets helpfulness, not gullibility. The elicitor never asks for the secret directly; they ask around it: 'I am new here, who handles the VPN issues?' → 'Oh, Marcus does, marcus.j@...' → each answer builds the org chart for the next attack. Techniques include flattery ('you clearly know how things really work here'), feigned ignorance ('I am so lost with this new system'), and the false statement ('so the backups run on Fridays, right?' — corrected to the true schedule by a helpful employee). Defenses: the 'need-to-know pause' (before answering, ask 'why do they need this and who are they?'), and deflecting to public channels ('that is on our website' or 'let me connect you with our office manager'). Physical security drills make this concrete: hire or role-play a friendly visitor attempting tailgating and information elicitation, then debrief — the receptionist who challenged the visitor becomes the example, praised publicly. Visitor policy in plain terms, posted at the desk: every visitor signs in, wears a badge, is escorted beyond the lobby, and the Wi-Fi password is never given verbally to unverified visitors. And the clean-USB rule with its reasoning explained: 'Unknown USB devices go to IT unopened — not because we distrust you, but because attackers count on curiosity, and IT has safe ways to check.' Rules with reasons get followed; rules without reasons get resented and bypassed.

notes.title: Why smart people click: the psychology attackers rent
notes.body: Phishing works on smart people because it rents well-studied decision shortcuts, not because victims are foolish. Authority: we comply with perceived authority figures — the fake CEO's 'urgent wire transfer,' the fake IT admin's instructions. Urgency and scarcity: time pressure shuts down deliberation — 'respond in 24 hours or your account is suspended' is designed to make you act before you think. Social proof: 'your colleagues have already completed the survey' — nobody wants to be the holdout. Reciprocity: the attacker gives first — a helpful 'IT support' call, a free gift — creating a vague obligation to comply. Curiosity and greed: 'see who viewed your profile,' 'claim your refund.' Liking and familiarity: the message that mirrors your writing style, references your real projects, or comes from a compromised colleague's actual account. Spearphishing layers these with reconnaissance: your job title from LinkedIn, your vendor names from a breach, your manager's name from the company site — each true detail makes the false request feel verified. Teaching this honestly matters: when users understand they were manipulated by design rather than 'stupid,' shame drops and reporting rises — and reporting is the metric you actually want. Worked example — mapping levers to a single lure: 'Hi, I am Sarah from HR (authority + familiarity). We are updating emergency contacts and most of the team has finished (social proof). Please complete yours by 5 PM today so payroll is not delayed (urgency). As a thank-you, the first fifty get a gift card (reciprocity + greed).' Five levers in four sentences — that is why it works, and naming them aloud is the inoculation. Common mistakes in awareness training: mocking victims (kills reporting instantly); presenting attackers as hooded geniuses (most phishing is industrial, templated, and unglamorous — which is scarier and more useful to know); and teaching 'look for bad grammar' as the primary defense (modern lures, especially AI-assisted ones, are grammatically flawless — teach verification habits, not typo-hunting). Inoculation theory — the research behind effective awareness training — says that exposing people to weakened versions of manipulation techniques builds resistance, the way a vaccine uses a weakened virus. That is the scientific case for phishing simulations and vishing drills done kindly: each safe exposure, followed by immediate teaching ('here is the lever they pulled'), strengthens the real-world response. It is also the case against fear-only training, which produces anxiety without skill. Frame training around the attacker's economics to demystify: phishing is industrial — templated kits, rented infrastructure, measured conversion rates. The attacker does not need to fool everyone; a 5% click rate on 10,000 emails is 500 footholds. Your defense does not need perfection either — it needs reporting fast enough that one click becomes one contained incident instead of one dwell-time disaster. Teach the 'scam anatomy' pattern across channels so the skill transfers: whether it is email, call, text, or visitor, the shape is the same — unsolicited contact + authority or urgency + a request that bypasses normal procedure + contact details they supply. 'Verify out-of-band' defeats all four uniformly, which is why it is the one habit worth repeating until it is reflex. A final psychology note for trainers: lead with respect. 'Attackers are professionals running an industry, and their techniques work on everyone including security people — here is how we beat them together' outperforms 'do not be the weak link' on every measure that matters, starting with attendance.

notes.title: Building the 30-minute awareness session
notes.body: A 30-minute session that changes behavior has a fixed architecture: hook, demo, habits, practice, close. Minutes 0-2, the hook: open with a real story, not statistics — 'Last quarter, someone in a company like ours wired $40,000 because an email looked like it came from their CEO. It took one phone call to have prevented it.' Stories create attention; statistics create yawns. Minutes 2-10, the live demo: dissect a real (sanitized) phishing email on screen, layer by layer — sender, urgency, link destination, attachment — exactly as taught in this module. Let the audience spot the red flags before you reveal them; participation beats lecture. Minutes 10-22, the habits: teach exactly three, because nobody retains seven. Habit 1: Pause — urgency is the tell; any message demanding immediate action gets a breath first. Habit 2: Verify through a known channel — do not use contact details from the suspicious message itself; call the internal help desk number, walk to the person's desk, start a new email to the known address. Habit 3: Report — show the report button or forwarding address live, and promise what happens next ('it goes to IT, you will get a thank-you, never blame'). Minutes 22-28, practice: a 5-question quiz on fresh examples — 'phish or legit?' with instant answers. Minutes 28-30, the close: one sentence to remember — 'When in doubt, verify out-of-band and report it; you will never be in trouble for reporting.' Logistics: schedule 30 minutes sharp and end on time (respect buys the next invitation); bring one printed handout (the three habits + reporting path on a single page); record it for new hires. Worked example — adapting for clinic staff: swap the wire-transfer story for a patient-data story ('a front-desk employee's login was used to access patient records after a fake IT call'), demo with a fake 'IT password reset' email instead of an invoice phish, and stress the HIPAA-adjacent stakes in plain words ('patient trust'). Common mistakes: jargon ('threat vector,' 'attack surface' — the audience leaves and retains nothing); the 90-minute slide marathon (attention is a budget — spend it); and ending without a clear reporting path (awareness without an action is trivia). Delivering the session remotely or to shift workers takes adaptation, not dilution. Remote: keep cameras encouraged but not mandatory, use polls for the 'phish or legit?' practice (everyone votes, then you reveal — participation without spotlight anxiety), and record for the night shift with the quiz as the attendance check. Shift workers: run the same 30 minutes at shift change twice rather than one 60-minute session nobody attends. New hires: the session belongs in week-one onboarding, before they develop inbox habits — plus a gentle simulated phish in week three as the inoculation dose. The handout design matters more than it seems: one page, large type, the three habits as numbered steps, the reporting path as a giant button-like box, and the after-click steps in a calm color. It lives taped to monitors and saved to phones — the thing people actually look at in the panicked moment. Reinforcement beats repetition: a monthly two-line 'scam of the month' email (one real example, one lever named, one reminder of the reporting path) keeps the habit warm between quarterly sessions far better than repeating the full training. And measure the session itself: a three-question pulse survey ('I know how to report a phish: yes/no,' 'I know what to do after clicking: yes/no,' 'one thing I will do differently: ___') tells you whether the 30 minutes worked and what to fix. Training that is never evaluated is a ritual; training with a feedback loop is a program.

notes.title: Teaching resistance: verify, report, no shame
notes.body: Resistance is not a personality trait — it is two habits plus a culture. Habit one, verify: any unexpected request for credentials, money movement, data, or access gets confirmed through an independent known channel. New email from the 'CEO' asking for gift cards? Start a fresh message to the CEO's known address, or walk over. Caller claiming to be IT? Hang up and call the help desk's published internal number. Text about a package? Go to the carrier's site directly, never the link. The rule is absolute and therefore teachable: never use contact details supplied by the suspicious message itself. Habit two, report: make reporting frictionless and visibly safe. One button or one forwarding address, advertised everywhere; every report gets acknowledged ('thanks — that was a phish, you did exactly right'); metrics celebrate reporters. The culture part is the hard one: no shame, ever. The employee who reports 'I clicked, I think it was bad' just gave you the earliest possible detection of a live intrusion — treat them like a hero, because functionally they are your best sensor. Punishing clickers teaches the whole company to hide the next incident, which is how a single clicked phish becomes a three-week dwell time. What to do after clicking: say it out loud in training — disconnect from the network, call IT immediately, do not try to fix it yourself, and change the password from a known-clean device. Worked example — the reporting loop done right: Maria gets a 'password expiry' email, hovers, sees a wrong domain, hits the report button. Within an hour IT confirms it is a credential phish, finds it reached 40 inboxes, purges it, and sends a two-line all-clear naming Maria's report as the catch. Next quarter, reporting rates double — because the company watched reporting work. Common mistakes: a report address nobody monitors (worse than no address — it teaches futility); public 'wall of shame' for clickers (destroys reporting culture permanently); and training that ends at 'do not click' without teaching the after-click response (someone will click — the plan must cover it). Executive sponsorship turns awareness from an IT chore into an organizational norm. When the clinic director opens the session with ninety seconds — 'I take this seriously, I do the simulations too, reporting is always safe here' — attendance, attention, and reporting all move. Ask for that sponsorship explicitly and make it easy: draft the ninety seconds for them. Reward structures beat punishment structures: a quarterly 'best catch' recognition (the reporter whose flag caught a real campaign), team reporting-rate leaderboards framed as collaboration, and visible follow-through ('because twelve of you reported this, we blocked it for everyone'). The help desk needs its own briefing, because reporters call them first: give the desk a one-page triage card (isolate? collect? escalate to whom? what to tell the user?) so the reporting loop does not die at the first human handoff. Integrate awareness with onboarding, offboarding, and role changes — access changes are the moments attackers exploit, so the human controls should move with them. And connect the program to the incident response plan: user reports should feed the detection phase explicitly ('user-reported phish' as a detection source in the IR playbook), with SLAs for triage. When a user's report triggers the IR process and the user hears back that their report mattered, you have closed the loop between awareness training and incident response — the two modules of this course shaking hands. That closed loop is the difference between a compliance checkbox and a living defense.

notes.title: Measuring honestly: click rates without lying to yourself
notes.body: The industry's favorite metric — phishing simulation click rate — is easy to game and easy to misread, so measure it like a scientist, not a marketer. Establish a baseline with your first simulation before any training, using a medium-difficulty lure; that number (say 28%) is your honest starting point. After training, re-test with a lure of equal difficulty — not an easier one, which manufactures improvement, and not a far harder one, which manufactures failure. Track three metrics, not one: click rate (did they click), reporting rate (did they report it — the metric you actually want to rise), and repeat-clicker rate (the same people clicking every time — your coaching list). Interpret with humility: a drop from 28% to 12% after training is real progress AND still means one in eight clicks — report both. Segment honestly: new hires click more (onboard them faster), and one department's 40% is a training opportunity, not a punishment target. Coach repeat clickers individually and kindly — a 10-minute conversation beats a fourth mandatory video. Never punish: punishment corrupts the metric (people stop reporting, click rates look better while real risk rises). Worked example — an honest quarterly report: 'Q3 simulation (medium difficulty, 212 employees): click rate 11%, down from 24% baseline; reporting rate 63%, up from 31%; 9 repeat clickers (down from 22) — all received 1:1 coaching. Caveat: this quarter's lure mimicked our benefits provider, which may have been slightly easier than baseline; next quarter we will re-test at baseline difficulty to confirm the trend.' That paragraph is credible because it volunteers its own weakness. Common mistakes: celebrating a 2% click rate on an obvious lure (vanity metric); comparing rates across different-difficulty lures (meaningless); naming and shaming departments (kills the reporting culture you are trying to build); and measuring once a year (skills decay — quarterly keeps the habit alive). Go one level deeper on honest statistics, because leadership will ask whether the program 'works' and you need a real answer. Significance basics: with 200 employees and a 10% click rate, the margin of error is roughly ±4% — so a move from 12% to 9% between quarters is noise, while 24% to 11% is signal. Say this out loud in the report; it builds credibility and prevents overreaction to wobbles. Control for difficulty explicitly: keep a small library of rated lures (easy/medium/hard, rated by a pilot group) and always compare within the same band. Track cohorts longitudinally: the same employees over time, not just company averages — averages hide the ten repeat clickers behind 190 improvers. Watch for the metrics that indicate gaming: reporting rates that fall while click rates fall (people hiding clicks), or suspiciously perfect scores from one department (answer-sharing). And correlate with reality: the ultimate metric is not simulation performance but real-world outcomes — user-reported real phish per quarter, mean time from user report to containment, and incidents with user-report as the detection source. When you can say 'user reports detected 40% of our real phishing incidents this year, up from 10%, with average report-to-containment under an hour,' you have proven the program in the only currency that matters. Present that alongside the simulation trends, keep the no-punishment rule sacrosanct, and the program funds itself — because nothing sells security investment like the workforce demonstrably functioning as a sensor network.

cards.front: Name the five layers of a phishing email's anatomy.
cards.back: Spoofed/lookalike sender → emotional subject → pretext → call to action (click/reply/open) → payload (fake login, malicious attachment, or wire fraud).

cards.front: What is display-name spoofing and why does it work?
cards.back: The attacker sets a trusted display name ('Acme Billing') over an unrelated address — most people read the name, not the address.

cards.front: What is vishing? Give the classic script.
cards.back: Voice phishing — e.g., the fake IT helpdesk call: 'suspicious logins on your account, read me the code on your phone' (stealing your MFA code).

cards.front: What is MFA fatigue (push bombing) and the defense?
cards.back: Spamming MFA approval prompts until the victim taps approve to stop the noise. Defense: number-matching MFA, and the rule to never approve unexpected prompts — report instead.

cards.front: Define pretexting, baiting, and tailgating in one line each.
cards.back: Pretexting: a fabricated scenario to extract info/access. Baiting: a tempting object (USB, download) that compromises. Tailgating: following someone through a secured door.

cards.front: Name four psychological levers phishers use.
cards.back: Authority, urgency/scarcity, social proof, reciprocity (plus curiosity/greed and liking/familiarity).

cards.front: What are the three habits taught in the 30-minute session?
cards.back: 1. Pause — urgency is the tell. 2. Verify through a known channel (never details from the suspicious message). 3. Report — and you will never be in trouble for reporting.

cards.front: Why is 'IT will never ask for your password or MFA code' such a powerful policy?
cards.back: It is simple, absolute, and testable — anyone can apply it in seconds, which makes the vishing script instantly recognizable.

cards.front: An employee reports 'I clicked, I think it was bad.' How do you respond?
cards.back: Like they are a hero: thank them, isolate and investigate immediately — they just gave you the earliest possible detection. Never punish.

cards.front: Name the three honest awareness metrics.
cards.back: Click rate, reporting rate (the one you want rising), and repeat-clicker rate (your coaching list).

cards.front: Why must re-tests use equal-difficulty lures?
cards.back: An easier lure manufactures fake improvement; a harder one manufactures fake failure. Only equal difficulty measures real change.

cards.front: What is the one sentence to close an awareness session with?
cards.back: 'When in doubt, verify out-of-band and report it; you will never be in trouble for reporting.'

quiz.q: An email from 'Acme Billing <billing@acme-billlng.com>' (double-l) urges payment within 24 hours via a 'Pay Now' button. How many red flags can you name, at minimum?
choices: Four: lookalike sender domain, urgency pressure, mismatched link destination, and the call-to-action pattern
One: the urgency alone proves nothing
Zero: the branding looks professional
Two: the subject line and the greeting
quiz.explain: Professional branding is copyable and proves nothing. Independent red flags compound: lookalike domain + urgency + link mismatch + unsolicited payment demand = conclusive.

quiz.q: 'This is IT — we see suspicious logins; read me the code on your phone to verify your identity.' What is actually happening?
choices: The attacker is completing a login as you using the MFA code you read aloud
IT is performing routine verification
Your phone is being hacked remotely
The code verifies the caller's identity
quiz.explain: The inversion is the tell: a legitimate verifier never asks you to surrender your own secret. The code is YOUR authentication — reading it hands over your session.

quiz.q: The correct response to an unsolicited 'IT support' call asking for credentials is:
choices: Hang up and call the help desk back on the published internal number
Debate the caller to waste their time
Call back the number the caller gave you
Comply, since they knew your name
quiz.explain: Engagement is the trap; callback numbers they supply ring the attacker; knowing your name is trivial reconnaissance. Verify through an independent known channel.

quiz.q: A visitor claiming to be a state inspector asks the front desk for the Wi-Fi password and a server-room tour. Best response?
choices: Verify the visit through the known internal channel (office manager) before granting anything
Grant Wi-Fi but not the tour
Ask to see the business card, then comply
Escort them immediately to be polite
quiz.explain: Pretexting is defeated by verifying through channels the visitor does not control. Business cards, uniforms, and confidence are props, not proof.

quiz.q: Why does shaming employees who click phishing simulations backfire?
choices: It teaches the whole company to hide future incidents instead of reporting them
It is illegal in most states
Click rates go up
Simulations become too easy
quiz.explain: Reporting is your early-warning system. Shame destroys it — the next real phish goes unreported and dwell time stretches from minutes to weeks.

quiz.q: In the 30-minute session architecture, what belongs in minutes 10-22?
choices: The three habits: pause, verify through a known channel, report
The hook story
The live phishing dissection demo
The attendee quiz
quiz.explain: Hook (0-2), demo (2-10), habits (10-22), practice quiz (22-28), close (28-30). Three habits maximum — nobody retains seven.

quiz.q: Your click rate fell from 24% to 11%, but this quarter's lure was easier than baseline. The honest report says:
choices: Report the numbers WITH the caveat, and re-test at baseline difficulty next quarter to confirm the trend
Celebrate the 11% as proven improvement
Discard the quarter's results entirely
Make next quarter's lure even easier
quiz.explain: Honest measurement volunteers its own weaknesses. Unequal difficulty makes the comparison suggestive, not conclusive — say so, then re-test properly.

quiz.q: Which metric best indicates a healthy reporting culture?
choices: Rising reporting rate — people flagging suspicious messages
Falling click rate alone
Zero clicks in a quarter
Fewer help-desk tickets
quiz.explain: Someone will always click; the reporting rate measures whether the organization detects it in minutes. A 0% click rate usually means the lure was too easy or people stopped engaging.

quiz.q: An employee clicked a real phish. What is the correct immediate advice?
choices: Disconnect from the network, call IT immediately, do not try to fix it, change the password from a clean device
Delete the email and hope for the best
Run a personal antivirus scan and continue working
Forward the phish to colleagues as a warning
quiz.explain: Contain (disconnect), escalate (call IT — speed matters), do not tamper with evidence, and rotate credentials from a trusted device. Forwarding spreads the phish.

quiz.q: A USB drive labeled 'Q3 Bonuses' is found in the parking lot. This is:
choices: Baiting — the label is engineered curiosity; do not plug it in; hand it to IT
A lucky find — check what is on it from your workstation
Probably harmless if antivirus is current
Safe if you only open the documents, not the executables
quiz.explain: Baiting exploits curiosity; 'only documents' is false safety (malicious macros, LNK exploits). The procedure is fixed: do not connect it, give it to IT.

items.prompt: Phishing via voice call?
items.explain: Voice phishing — e.g., the fake IT helpdesk script.

items.prompt: Phishing via SMS?
items.explain: Text-message lures: package delivery, bank alerts, toll notices.

items.prompt: Fabricated scenario to extract info?
items.explain: The 'auditor,' the 'vendor tech' — a story that justifies the request.

items.prompt: Following someone through a badge door?
items.explain: Physical access via politeness — counter with 'everyone badges in.'

items.prompt: Tempting object that compromises when used?
items.explain: The labeled USB drive, the 'free' download.

items.prompt: Attacker spams MFA prompts until victim approves?
items.explain: Defense: number-matching MFA; never approve unexpected prompts.

items.prompt: The absolute verification rule?
items.answer: Never use contact details from the suspicious message itself — verify through an independent known channel.
items.explain: Attacker-supplied numbers, links, and addresses all ring the attacker.

items.prompt: Someone clicked a real phish — first two actions?
items.answer: Disconnect from the network; call IT immediately.
items.explain: Contain, then escalate — speed beats self-repair attempts.

items.prompt: Email: 'Your mailbox is full — click here to upgrade storage.' Name the levers.
items.answer: Urgency/scarcity (mailbox full) + authority (IT-sounding sender) + curiosity about the link.
items.explain: Naming levers aloud is the inoculation — teach the pattern, not just the example.

items.prompt: A department head demands the names of repeat clickers 'for performance reviews.' Your answer?
items.answer: Decline: punishment destroys reporting culture; offer anonymized trends plus 1:1 coaching for repeat clickers instead.
items.explain: Protect the metric's integrity and the reporting culture — explain the dwell-time cost of fear.

items.prompt: Design a 5-question attendee quiz item testing the verification habit.
items.answer: 'You get a text from your "bank" about fraud with a link. What do you do?' Key: do not tap the link; open the bank app directly or call the number on your card.
items.explain: Good items test the habit (verify via known channel), not trivia.

items.prompt: A nurse says 'I do not have time for security training.' Your 20-second pitch?
items.answer: 'One fake IT call used a login like yours to open patient records at another clinic. Three habits — pause, verify, report — take thirty minutes once and protect your license and our patients.'
items.explain: Relevance (their world, their stakes) beats compliance language.

items.prompt: Reporting rate is flat at 20% after two quarters. Two fixes?
items.answer: Make reporting one click (friction kills it) and publicly celebrate catches — every report acknowledged, reporters praised by name (with permission).
items.explain: Reporting rises with ease and visible reward, not with more lectures.

items.prompt: The CEO wants the awareness session to be 90 minutes of slides. Your counter-proposal?
items.answer: 30 minutes sharp: hook story, live demo, three habits, practice quiz, close — plus the recording and one-page handout for everyone. Respect buys the next invitation.
items.explain: Attention is a budget; a tight 30 minutes that ends on time outperforms a 90-minute marathon nobody retains.

handsOnLab.title: Build and dry-run a 30-minute awareness session kit
handsOnLab.brief: You will produce a complete, deliverable awareness session kit — timed agenda, speaker notes, one-page handout, and a 5-question attendee quiz with answer key — then dry-run it against the clock. This is portfolio evidence and directly usable at the clinic.
steps: Write the session agenda with minute marks: hook (0-2), live demo (2-10), three habits (10-22), practice quiz (22-28), close (28-30).
Draft the hook: a 90-second real-pattern story (wire fraud via fake CEO email, or a fake IT call leading to a breach) — no statistics, one story.
Build the demo script: take the fake-invoice phish anatomy from the notes and write presenter lines that let the audience spot each red flag before you reveal it.
Write speaker notes for the three habits (pause, verify through a known channel, report) — one short paragraph each, zero jargon.
Design the one-page handout: the three habits, the reporting path (button/address), and the after-click steps (disconnect, call IT, clean-device password change).
Write the 5-question attendee quiz: each item a mini-scenario testing a habit, with an answer key and one-line teaching explanation per answer.
Adapt one example for a non-technical audience (clinic front desk): rewrite it using their world and stakes.
Dry-run aloud with a timer: read the full script and mark where you land at 10, 22, and 28 minutes — cut or tighten to hit the marks.
Record the honesty-metrics slide: baseline plan, three metrics (click, reporting, repeat-clicker), equal-difficulty re-test rule, no-punishment policy.
Assemble awareness-session-kit.md: agenda, speaker notes, handout text, quiz + key, metrics plan.
Read the kit as a skeptical nurse with zero security background: circle every unexplained term and rewrite it.
Final check: could a colleague deliver this session from your kit alone tomorrow? If not, fill the gaps.
handsOnLab.deliverable: awareness-session-kit.md — timed agenda, speaker notes, one-page handout text, 5-question attendee quiz with key, and the honest measurement plan.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: The kit is timed to 30 minutes, contains zero unexplained jargon, the handout fits one page, the quiz tests habits (not trivia) with a key, and the metrics plan includes the equal-difficulty and no-punishment rules.

videos.blurb: The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency's official channel publishes public awareness videos on phishing, social engineering, and protective habits.

mockTask.q: Panel question: A clinic manager asks, 'How would you teach phishing awareness to our front-desk staff, who are not technical at all?' What is your plan?
choices: A 30-minute session: a real-story hook, a live dissection of a fake IT email where they spot the red flags, three habits (pause, verify through a known channel, report), a 5-question practice quiz, and a one-page handout — measured later with honest equal-difficulty simulations and no punishment
A 90-minute slide deck covering every attack type in technical detail
Monthly phishing tests with public shaming of anyone who clicks
Tell them to look for bad grammar and misspelled words in emails
mockTask.explain: The panel wants audience-appropriate design: short, story-led, participatory, habit-focused, with a takeaway and honest measurement. Slide marathons do not change behavior, shaming destroys reporting, and typo-hunting fails against modern lures.
